CONGRATULATIONS TO PENTICTON V'S ON REGAINING WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to the splendid achievement of the Penticton V's in regaining the world amateur hockey championship for Canada. These players deserve the congratulations of all Canadians on their splendid teamwork during all the international games. I hope that all hon. members present will join me in thanking the Penticton Y's for a task well done.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS TO PENTICTON V'S ON REGAINING WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP
speechtext:
On the
question of privilege, I associate myself with what has been said, and I know the hon. gentleman himself and the whole house will join with me, and the hon. gentleman would not want it to go without saying that, as an example of co-operation and teamwork in achieving this splendid victory, recognition should be given to the part played on the Penticton team by defencemen Middleton and Taggart from the hon. gentleman's own city of Kelowna, and my city of Kamloops, respectively.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS TO PENTICTON V'S ON REGAINING WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP
speechtext:
I know that all hon. members will agree with the sentiments expressed by both the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary and the hon. member for Kamloops.
I must say that I am not a very ardent hockey fan, but I watched with great enthusiasm the various games shown on the television screen by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation last week, and I was very glad and deeply proud of the success which has been achieved by the Penticton team and those from the riding of Kamloops who have reinforced the team from time to time.
Anticipating your feelings, I this morning sent a telegram to His Worship the Mayor of Penticton, which reads as follows:
All Canadians very proud of Penticton hockey team. Heartiest congratulations to our world champions, their families and yourself.
From what I could see on the television screen, all teams who participated in those games are to be congratulated on the true sportsmanship that they have shown; that
is in itself good not only for those who were members of the various teams but also for all nations that have sent teams there. We do congratulate our new world hockey champions most heartily.

1. Has a decision been reached	by the	government to conduct a nation-wide census in 1956?
2. If so, will complete information ordinarily obtained by the census in the prairie provinces be collected?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could answer this question verbally. Hon. members will recall that it is a constitutional requirement that a quinquennial census of the prairie provinces be taken in 1956. There have been numerous developments in Canada in recent years which point to the need for bringing all provinces into the census survey in 1956.
The rapid growth of the Canadian population and shifts within and between provinces have posed problems of great difficulty for provincial and municipal administration and for business.
Censuses of agriculture provide the base on which annual estimates of crops and livestock are calculated through annual mail sample inquiries. The greater diversity of agricultural practices makes it difficult to keep estimates in line unless this base is provided more frequently than every ten years. This is particularly true in those parts of Canada where agriculture is more diversified.
However it is not considered to be essential to take a quinquennial census on the scale of the decennial. A simplified census in 1956 should meet most needs. It is not necessary to obtain information every five years concerning those characteristics of the population that are fairly stable, such as religion, origin, education and place of birth.
Orders for Returns
It is proposed to ask only five population questions, in addition to the name and address: age, sex, marital status, relationship to head of household and whether living on a farm. In 1951 there were 29 questions on the population card. The census of agriculture would be reduced from 200 questions in 1951 to 75 in 1956.
Hon. members will be asked to provide the necessary funds at the time the estimates for the Department of Trade and Commerce are presented for consideration.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the public reports that proven polio vaccine of Canadian origin is being made available to grades 1 and 2 in our schools before the polio danger season arrives, is the minister aware that in all likelihood proven vaccine of United States manufacture will shortly be available in this country in substantial quantities, and is the government prepared to arrange for its distribution on the same basis as the Canadian vaccine, or will it only be available through commercial houses to those who can afford it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISTRIBUTION OF VACCINE
speechtext:
My hon. friend did not give me notice of his intention to ask this question. Although I do not say that he is required to give notice, my answer cannot be as complete as it would if he had done so. As I have intimated in this house during the course of the present session the federal government in co-operation with the provinces has made arrangements for distribution of this vaccine on a trial basis. My hon. friend is also aware, of course, that the basic production of the Salk vaccine has taken place to the extent of 90 per cent at the Connaught laboratories in Toronto, partly as a result of assistance given under the national health program. I may assure my hon. friend that the various provincial departments of health and the Department of National Health and Welfare in a co-operative enterprise have been aware of the importance of this particular vaccine and are taking every step to make certain that Canadian children and Canadian citizens generally will have the full advantage of this vaccine if and when the final assessment reveals it to be of beneficial purpose.
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISTRIBUTION OF VACCINE
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Has the government pursued the question as to whether or not United States vaccine will be available in Canada at approximately the same date?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISTRIBUTION OF VACCINE
speechtext: My hon. friend asks me whether or not we will use United States vaccine. I am convinced that his question is falsely based. I have indicated that almost 90 per cent of the production of vaccine is taking place at the Connaught laboratories, an institution of great note, at the University of Toronto. Therefore it is erroneous to talk about a United States vaccine. Dr. Salk, it is true, was an American medical scientist who made the discovery, but it is not exact to talk of it as a United States vaccine. I cannot answer my hon. friend more adequately than to say we are aware of the situation, and just as soon, as the University of Michigan has made the necessary assessment no loss of time will take place in Canada in making this particular vaccine available for use if it is thought to be of value in the final analysis, as we all hope and anticipate it will be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lapointe for the second reading of Bill No. 164, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
On Friday last, just before the closing of the house, I was making some remarks
(Mr. Kirk (Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare).]

on the bill which is now before us. I believe I emphasized the fact that the men who qualify for war veterans allowance are those men who served in France in the first great war and who are generally over 60 years of age and unable to do steady work. They are in extremely difficult circumstances before they become eligible for this allowance. I believe I also pointed out, as did other members during the course of the debate on Friday, that the unwounded survivors of the trench warfare of 1914-18 had undergone exposure and hazards which could easily impair their physical vigour. I then drew attention to the fact that the financial burden on the country was not likely to be increased because the numbers eligible for war veterans allowance were being seriously depleted with each succeeding year. Going on from that point I draw the attention of the house to the fact that the war veterans allowance board deals with seven types of person: veterans generally over 60 years of age who served in world war I and who number 25,038; veterans of world war II who number 2,199; then 511 veterans of two wars; commonwealth and allied veterans who number 2,902; dependents who number 829; widows who number 10,706 and 131 orphans or a grand total of 42,316 persons on whose behalf the sum of $26,846,086.98 was expended during the last fiscal year. However, the main body of this total is found in the 25,038 veterans of world war I. They are the persons for whom this act was devised and are the largest group of beneficiaries.
On Friday I pointed out that approximately 400,000 Canadians served overseas in France during world war I. Of these, 60,000 were killed; 180,000 were wounded; and 160,000 survived unwounded. How many of the wounded and unwounded are living today? Departmental figures show that over the years more than 100,000 persons have appeared on their lists of those drawing disability pensions. At the present time that number has been reduced to 62,000. Since 1930 about 60,000 persons on war veterans allowance have died. That means that of these 340,000 survivors of the Canadian expeditionary force, about one-third have died since the war. Probably the figure is higher. The remaining 200,000 or so will not last much longer. The average age of veterans of world war I is 65. The expectation of life at age 65 is just over 13 years. By the end of this parliament and the next two parliaments the problem of war veterans allowance for world war I veterans will have been practically solved through the death of these survivors. However, my hope is that it can be solved during this present parliament.

I think it is a disgrace that almost 40 years after -world war I we are still tinkering with the serious problem of the veterans of that war. Forty years ago these men for whom we are now making a plea flocked to the colours. They received an outfit of clothing, two blankets and a ground sheet, $1.10 a day and some of the poorest food that was ever concocted in the history of mankind. After the war they were very much on their own. There were in existence no large schemes for rehabilitation such as those with which we have become familiar since this second war. No university courses were offered or no payments while awaiting returns for those entering business. There was just a small gratuity. Those men faced disappointment in the early years owing to unemployment and low wages. There was no post-war boom. By the end of 1929, just when many of them were getting on their feet, the great ten-year depression struck. Then along came the second world war in which many of them served, either in the active army or in the veterans guard. Ten years of war! Ten years of depression! What more could be asked from one generation? The wonder is that there are only 25,000 on war veterans allowance. Many of these men never had a real chance during the best years of their lives.
Now what are they offered? They are offered $60 a month for single men and $108 for married men; no increase in permissive income for single men; only $2 a month for married men; ceilings of $840 and $1,440.
As reported at page 1731 of Hansard the minister says this:
We believe that the new ceilings are capable of allowing recipients to maintain a reasonable level of subsistence.
The key word there is "subsistence". Two wars, a depression, 60 years of age, intermittent or no employment and "subsistence": this for men who served in the trenches in France!
The other day I opened the book of estimates for this year just at random. The page was headed "Civil Service Commission" and I came across an item which read, "Office boys and girls", starting annual salary, $1,080. There you have the situation: at the commencement of a career, an office boy, $1,080; at the end of years of service, a 60-year-old or older veteran, with active service in France, $840 or, if married, $1,440 provided he can still earn. If unable to work, the figures are, of course, $720 and $1,296.
The minister's remarks the other day I thought were cold, unsympathetic, confusing and unconvincing. He attempted to equate the ceilings of war veterans allowance with the rates for disability pensions. What purpose this procedure served I am at a loss to
War Veterans Allowance Act know. He then went on to estimate the additional cost to the treasury if the ceilings were placed at $1,200 and $2,000. He estimated that these would open the way to placing 14,750 new applicants on the rolls and would increase the cost by $13 million over and above the present proposed increase.
This is a familiar dodge practised by some cabinet ministers. We are supposed to accept these statements as gospel truth. No detailed analysis was given by the minister. All that was given was just a bland assurance that this would be the result and that consequently there was no further argument. I hope that the committee will pursue this matter and get a detailed breakdown of these figures. We need to know the number of single men on war veterans allowance and the number of married men. We need to know a great deal about their present income and things of that nature. These facts are not available to the members of the house. We cannot challenge the statements made by the minister and hence we are met with some large figure like that which is intended to demolish all argument.
I regret that the recommendation of the Canadian Legion has not been accepted in full. Over all these many years the Canadian Legion, the navy, army and air force veterans and other veterans organizations have done their best to make more endurable the life of the veteran. It is as a result of their effort that the veterans of world war II have received better treatment than those of world war I. The Canadian Legion's suggestions year after year have been reasonable and just. No attempt has ever been made to raid the treasury. No extravagant demands have been put forward.
But without the patient years of labour of the veterans of world war I the present veterans charter would be but a pale shadow. From time to time even that charter requires alteration and amendment. Let it be done quickly. I urge the minister to settle the problem of the veterans of world war I. Time is running out; it will soon be too late to do justice to these men. How quickly we forget. I do not wish to be too critical of the minister. The events of the first world war occurred before his time, certainly before he was able to understand war. Nevertheless from the knowledge he gained in the second great war it should not be difficult for him to visualize the trials and tribulations of the men of the Canadian corps from 1914 to 1918. I submit if that is not understood it is impossible to approach the problem of the men who are receiving the war veterans allowance.

War Veterans Allowance Act
There was a great difference between the two world wars. From the time the Canadians went to France in the spring of 1915 until the summer of 1918, over a period of three and a half years their life consisted of trench warfare and infantry battles. They were engaged in a defensive struggle and a war of attrition. They fought battle after battle merely to blunt the German offensive or to straighten the trench line or by limited offensives to weaken their opponents. Casualties were on an immense scale. Endurance was tested to the limit. There was nothing in the second world war comparable to these engagements in 1915, 1916, 1917 and the first half of 1918. Only the tragedies of Dieppe and Hong Kong bear any resemblance to the bitter struggles of those early years.
There was nothing in the second world war that remotely resembled the Ypres salient, that salient in which one million men of the British commonwealth died, not to mention the millions of wounded, that salient in which each Canadian division served in turn, that salient in which the first Canadian division endured without protection the gas attack of 1915, that salient that will be remembered forever because of Passchendaele. Let us not forget that it was in March, 37 years ago, that the allied forces were in as great danger as at any time during the second world war. That was the month in which Haig issued his famous order: "Our backs are to the wall." That was the month in which the Canadian soldiers were ordered to hold their position to the last man and the last round. That was the month in which a regiment of the Canadian cavalry, the Lord Strathcona's Horse, made its famous attack on Moreuil Wood in which Lieutenant Flower-dew won the Victoria Cross. That was the month just 37 years ago that the crisis of the first great war occurred.
The cost in human life and suffering staggers the imagination. Consider, for example, the long drawn out battle of the Somme in the fall of 1916. For a period of three months the four Canadian divisions took their turn in that battle so aptly described by the Germans as the "blood bath". After three months' fighting they had gained 4,000 yards, a little over 2J miles, with a loss of 24,000 men. It was after that battle that Lloyd George wrote these words:
The Canadians played a part of such distinction that thenceforward they were marked out as storm troops: for the remainder of the war they were brought along to head the assault in one great battle after another. Whenever the Germans found the Canadian corps coming into the line the; prepared for the worst.
In the summer of 1918 the war took a turn for the better and from then to its conclusion,


that is, during the celebrated last 100 days, the war in France and Flanders of 1914 to 1918 resembled the war that was fought by the Canadians in the second great war in northwest Europe. It was a war of movement with the allies being on the offensive, enjoying air supremacy, and moving steadily forward towards victory. Arthur Bryant, writing in the Illustrated London News of the 30th of October, 1954, states that the battle of Amiens on the 8th of August, 1918, was one of the great decisive battles in the history of the world. Ludendorff called it "the black day of the German army". That was the battle in which the Canadian corps spearheaded the advance of the British armies and inflicted a crushing defeat on the German forces.
I remind the minister of some of these episodes of the first great war. I remind him of the loss endured by the Canadian corps, of the casualties suffered, of the great expenditure of effort and of life. The men who performed these feats of endurance and of valour were the men of the Canadian corps of the first world war. Among the survivors of that period are the 62,000 disability pensioners still on our list and the 25,000 men drawing war veterans allowance. A grateful country could not begin to repay the debt owed to these men, but it is still not too late to make some amends for the neglect of past years. There is still time for the minister to recognize the achievements of these men and to grant them some contribution to lighten the troubles of increasing age. Among the 25,000 men on the list of those drawing war veterans allowance, there surely must be some who were present at the gas attack at Ypres, some who were present at the attack at Courcellette, at Vimy Ridge, at Hill 70, at Passchendaele, at Amiens, Canal du Nord and other battles of that first war. The list of engagements in which these men took part would make interesting reading.
No one who visits the memorial chamber in this building and reads the record inscribed on its walls can fail to be impressed by the accomplishments of Canada's soldiers of the first great war. On panel No. 1 just at the left as you enter the chamber there are inscribed these words:
Read how free men throughout this land kept faith in the hour of trial and in the day of battle, remembering the traditions they had been taught, counting life nothing without liberty.
Then on the fourth panel within that chamber may be found the following:
They are too near to be great but our children shall understand when and how our fate was changed and by whose hand. Nor was their agony brief or once only imposed on them; the wounded.

the warspent, the sick received no exemption; being cured they returned and endured and achieved our redemption.
Although, Mr. Speaker, those words are in honour of those who died, they represent something of what the survivors endured, too. I make my plea on behalf of those who are now on war veterans allowance. Let Canada pay generously and immediately some small part of the debt that this great nation owes to these men.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only rise to give further support to what has been said so ably by other members on this side of the house. I too feel, in fact I know, a grave injustice is being done to some very brave and true Canadian returned men. I do not believe any member in this house would oppose a move to increase war veterans allowances by $10 per month as envisaged by this bill. The injustice which has been done lies in the fact that under this bill there has been no proper increase in the maximum annual income plus allowances allowed to the veterans, whether single or married.
The present figure of $840 for single men, being the total annual income plus allowances before a man can qualify, is in this day and age unjust. The total annual income plus allowances for a married man is $1,440, and that is also an injustice with the cost of living where it is today. People cannot live decently on that amount of money. The fault lies with the government of this country because a few years ago they refused to maintain the controls which would have kept the cost of living down. Had the cost of living been kept at the point it was 40 years ago when these men stood at the breaches in Germany, these amounts would have sufficed. But with the cost of living having doubled in the last 15 years, $840 means very little.
As a delegate to the annual Legion conference held in Toronto last August, I know how these men felt. I know the feeling of the delegates from the various parts of Canada who went to this conference. The matter of war veterans allowances was one of the things these boys placed at the top of their agenda. Something should be done to see that these men under war veterans allowance are taken care of for the few years left to them. All branches of the Legion across Canada have endorsed this move in asking the government to make this increase. The government failed to do so. I do not believe that the act in its present form is fulfilling what even the Canadian people would want to be done for the men who defended us.

The government itself considers that a single man requires $1,000 per year upon which to live, and they set that as the amount of income he must have before he becomes liable for income tax. The amount is $2,000 for a married man. Surely these veterans, who gave so much of their youth and who have suffered so much that they are less able to earn for themselves, should be allowed at least $1,000 minimum for single men and $2,000 for married men.
This bill is going to the committee. The committee will be made up of members from all sides of the house but the majority will be members from the government side. I know that the members from the opposition parties will urge that changes should be made and these maxima should be increased; but when the vote is taken, the decision will be made according to what the government members on that committee do. Canada will be watching. Canadians and the Legion will judge this parliament by the amendments which are brought in by this committee. Government members, particularly last Friday, time after time extolled what the government had done for the veterans. I will agree that the government has done some good things. However, by allowing the cost of living to increase, they have been doing an injustice to the people of Canada and particularly to those veterans who are unable to earn a living for themselves. The proposed increase in allowances does not make up, by any means, for the increased cost of living.
Somebody said in this debate that the Canadian veterans legislation is the best in the world. This was set right in the last issue of The Legionary when it was pointed out that there are countries which have better legislation than we have in Canada. A single man with 100 per cent disability in Canada receives $125 monthly, while in the United States the rate is $181. A married man with a 100 per cent disability in Canada receives $170 while the United States rate is $202 per month. The government, however, should take a step at this time to raise the amounts of the Canadian scheme for veterans, and make it one of the best. I would urge the committee, therefore, to take hold of this legislation and bring it back with amendments which will go so far as to make the maximum for single men $1,000 per annum and for married men $2,000 per annum.
Remember, as the speaker before me has said so well, these men offered their lives and, today, worn and many unable to earn a living, they ask only a small amount immediately so that they may live decently. We should not do less than that. If we do, then

It is
not my purpose to speak at length. I do feel, however, it is fitting that I make a few remarks. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), in what I consider one of the finest speeches I have ever listened to in this house, rendered further talking almost unnecessary. Far too long Canadians have shabbily treated many of our soldiers of former wars. It is long past the time when we should begin to regard our less fortunate veterans as free Canadians with a right to the abundance of good things Canada produces. Today, we treat them as though they were a special class who had committed some sort of crime, by reason of which they are being denied the good things of life in Canada-a most astounding situation.
The recipients of war veterans allowances have been among the less fortunate of our veterans. These men, in the days of their youth and health and vigour and high hopes, arose in their country's time of need. Every heart in Canada was shaken with fear. They arose and marched and stood, sufficient in their generation. What we are doing in this parliament in rewarding them is far from being sufficient in our generation. Those men flinched not in the hour of testing. Members of this parliament are flinching by reason of the fear of a measly $5 million.

speechtext:
Peanuts is right; peanut shells!
Why should the lovely girls, who to those boys gave themselves for better or for worse, be condemned indefinitely to wear threadbare, mediocre dresses, hand-me-down overcoats; to deprive themselves of the health-giving foods, to stint themselves in respect of the many little indulgences that so much contribute to the enjoyability of life?
Well, those girls as wives never again will know what it means to live freely. I say, Mr. Speaker, just as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said, it is a disgrace that things of this sort should be done to those women who married those heroes of ours.
Every man who fought for Canada is entitled to a living-and I mean a living-in comfort and peace of mind. Those men do not know what the meaning of living is, nor of comfort, nor of peace of mind. I refer to the men who are on war veterans allowance. The men on war veterans allowance do not have comfort; they do not have peace of mind.

Canadian production is now around $24 billion a year, over $1,500 worth of goods, not money, a year for every individual. Canadian capacity to increase production of food, clothing, shelter, entertainment, health services and culture is well-nigh limitless. Do you not think that anybody with any degree of intelligence at all would say: now, if we are not producing enough of these good things for these men, let us by all means produce it and see that they get their share of it. Instead of that, we refuse to produce it and refuse to give them a share, the kind of share which they require and should have.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that any government that fails to provide for Canadian veterans on veterans allowance appropriate comfort and peace of mind is betraying its trust to Canadians, not only to the men who are concerned.
No more, I think, needs to be said, except that it is high time that men started considering how to distribute the goods we produce. The prices of agricultural products are falling today because there are not sufficient markets, there is not enough money in consumers' hands to buy the goods. Consequently, there is a tendency to decrease the production. Well, why not put money into the hands of those veterans so that they can increase consumption, at least as far as their needs will permit?
I shall have no more to say at the present time, but I certainly do hope that before we leave this parliament this year something far better than is contemplated in this bill will be worked out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the remarks that have been made during this debate, I am not quite certain whether I shall be held up as a horrible example or as the exception which proves the rule. I am not going to go into a discussion of that but one day I hope to debunk the Pearkes myth. I am just an ordinary person who happened to be rather lucky. I was lucky in this respect. When I came back from the first war I had a position open and available for me, and therefore I did not have to go through the very difficult period of becoming rehabilitated after the first world war.
Hon. members will recall the days of 1920 when so many of our men came back. It was one of the craziest periods in all history. It was a period of jazz and cocktail parties and rum-runners. It was in that atmosphere that men who had been through years of trench warfare had to readjust themselves to civilian life. Men who had left this country while still in their teens came back and had to look for a job. It was toward the end of that period when representations were
fMr. Castleden.]

made, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). Pressure was brought upon the government to do something for those men who, while perhaps not visibly wounded, still had suffered terribly from the effects of those years in trench warfare.
I am not going to repeat what the hon. member for Royal has already put on the record, namely, quotations from that great conference of veterans at Saint John, quotations from that great leader, Brigadier General Ross, who was president of the Canadian Legion. Remember, in those early days when the men came back, there was no Canadian Legion to give them hope and stability. All those things were different after the second world war.
To deal particularly with this bill, I should like to recall the words which were uttered by the Minister of Veterans Affairs in this house on February 22. When speaking on this bill he said that the increases would raise appreciably the standard of living of many veterans and their dependents. That went out all across the country. These men who had been suffering for years, and had been struggling along on a pittance, had high hopes that they were going to have their standard of living raised appreciably. Then, a few hours afterwards, the bill was introduced. The standard of living is going to be raised! The cost of living has been raised many times. This bill was going to raise the standard of living by increasing the amount of money which a single man could earn, plus his allowance, from $720 to $840, and he was expected in one year to see a big increase in the standard of his living on the princely sum of $840. If he was married and he and his wife were living together, the standard of living of the veteran and his wife was going to be raised appreciably by the magnificent increase from $1,200 to $1,440 a year. That is the maximum amount that he was allowed to earn. Then during his remarks on second reading the minister uttered words which have been quoted already in the very moving address by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). The minister said, as reported on page 1731 of Hansard of March 4:
We believe that the new ceilings are capable of allowing recipients to maintain a reasonable level of subsistence.
How preposterous! How can you have a reasonable level of subsistence on $1,440 a year. The new ceilings provide $2 a month increase in permissible income for a married couple. Magnificent, is it not? Then in closing the minister said:
I am convinced that it will be of great help to our older veterans.
War Veterans Allowance Act
What a great help it will be, $2 per month. At the annual meeting in Toronto last year of the Canadian Legion the minister apologized for making what he considered to be a master understatement. He certainly needs to apologize now for having made the overstatement of all time when he describes these miserable increases as being of great help to the older veterans and as raising appreciably their standard of living. I could go on expressing these sentiments because I feel deeply the insult which has been added to the long period of procrastination which has occurred in looking after these older veterans. However, as I feel that the speeches of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre have dealt thoroughly with this matter I shall go on to deal with one or two smaller points.
First of all, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), in his paeans of praise for the various cabinet ministers, forgot the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). I think he might have included the Minister of National Revenue because after all it is the responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue to collect the money from the taxpayers to pay for these increases. These increases will not come out of any secret fund of the Liberal party, although from the praise which was given by the hon. member for Vancouver South one might have thought that it is the Liberal ministers who are going to take this money out of their own pockets for these increases. The fact is that the money comes from the Canadian taxpayer and I believe that this is one case where the Canadian taxpayer would be pleased to show his appreciation of what these men have gone through.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) gave some incorrect and confusing information when he was speaking the other night about the widows of imperial veterans. Referring to the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod), the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said, as reported on page 1751 of Hansard of March 4:
The previous speaker referred to the widows of imperial veterans not getting a break because some of them had been in this country for 19 years and 360 days. That is too bad;-
Then he finishes up with this statement:
Those who fall within that bracket are going to have to wait just as the widow of the imperial war veteran, referred to by the previous speaker, will have to wait. All people like this will be deprived of legislative benefits until they are here for the necessary period of 20 years.
The hon. member completely missed the point. Under the present legislation the widow of an imperial veteran will have to

War Veterans Allowance Act wait until doomsday before she will get a penny. These widows do not get war veterans allowance after being residents for 20 years. That is the whole point of the plea made by us on this side, that these women should receive consideration when they reach the age of 55 years and when they have been in this country for 20 years. We argue that they should be treated as any other war widow and be entitled to a war veterans allowance irrespective of the fact that their husbands may have died before having lived here for 20 years. The widow would have to live here for 20 years and would have to reach the age of 55 the same as anyone else.
We are not asking for any special consideration; we are simply asking for fair play. How long does one have to live in this country before he becomes a Canadian? Do these widows of imperial veterans, although they have lived here for 20 years, still have to be treated as second-class Canadians? That is exactly what the government is doing. Many of them sent their sons overseas with the Canadian forces during the second world war. Some were born in Canada.
There is one other point I should like to raise, the matter of liquid assets or the money a veteran may have in the bank or in investment funds. Some of these men have been saving every penny they can in order to set aside something for their declining years. A man may run into bad luck or reach a time when he is unable to work and feel that he must fall back on the war veterans allowance. If he has accumulated any savings he is told that he must reduce his liquid assets to $1,000 if single or to $2,000 if married. Just think what that means. These people have been saving ever since the first war 35 years ago, they have been scraping together everything they can in case catastrophe should occur during the last years of their lives.
If the veterans who are single have bank savings of a few dollars more than the minimum of $1,000 or $2,000 in the case of a married man, they are told that if they want to receive the war veterans allowance that they should spend the money, buy a T.V. set or anything they like, but in any event cut down their savings to the $1,000 or $2,000 mark, and then we will give them the war veterans allowance. We ask them to reverse the principles which they have followed all through their lives in trying to be independent and trying to save up their money and not squander every penny they have earned. We tell them to go and spend their money and reduce their assets and bring them down to the $1,000 or $2,000 mark. These men are put in an inferior
[Mr. Pearkes.l

position to those who receive old age assistance. The person who applies for old age assistance has his liquid assets based on an annuity basis. His liquid assets are converted to this annuity basis, that is to say, what the liquid assets will buy in the form of a ten-year annuity payable monthly. I can give you examples to illustrate how that basis of reckoning the liquid assets for the old age assistance is more favourable than the war veterans allowance to an individual.
I know of a case involving a widow who is between the ages of 65 and 70. She owns a home, if you can call it a home. It is actually a cottage assessed at the value of $2,450. In addition to that she possesses liquid assets of $1,700. Now, based on an annuity basis under the old age assistance, the maximum income from all sources is $65 less rental assessment of $10, less annuity assessment of $10. Therefore the old age assistance plus the cost of living bonus amounts to $45 per month. If she had previously applied for the war veterans allowance she would not have been allowed to receive war veterans allowance although she is entitled to it according to all service requirements. She has been told that she must wait until she reduces her liquid assets of $1,700. She must wait until that total is brought down to $1,000.
I know of another case involving a single man between the ages of 65 and 70. He does not own a home but he does possess liquid assets of $4,000. He is able to qualify for the old age assistance and he receives $35 a month but he cannot receive war veterans allowance because he has liquid assets of $4,000. If he goes out and buys a T.V. set and that sort of thing and can reduce those hard-earned savings of a lifetime to $1,000, then, and only then, will he be eligible for the war veterans allowance.
I know that this bill is to be referred to the committee. I know that representations will be made both by members of this house and by the representatives of the great veterans organizations across the country. We can only hope that, in view of the representations which are now being made here on the floor of this house and in view of those representations which will be made before the committee, the government will see its way clear to extend the benefits which may be obtained under this new legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take very many minutes in making my remarks. I do want to rise and tell the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) that I welcome this legislation. It might be a little late in coming but I am delighted to see it coming into being. It is difficult to participate in the debate at this

time without repeating what someone else has said, because everything has been well covered. My colleagues in this group, who no doubt will be on the committee too, have pretty well expressed my views and I do not need to go into them at length. When it comes to legislation of this kind you will find that political lines disappear altogether. We tend to forget what party we belong to. Perhaps it is fortunate that we do not have too much time in which to discuss this bill. Whereas my colleague from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) attempted to tell us that the Kootenay Cougars won the war, and whereas my hon. friend from VancoUver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) gave the credit to the 46th division, I know that 36 or 37 years ago I was firmly convinced that the 51st division won the war. Nobody could have convinced me at that time that we did not win it. However, I know that everyone in this house is going to support this legislation.
It has been said that this is the finest legislation in the world. In a country like this, why shouldn't it be? This is the finest country in the world, and we should have the finest veterans legislation. When we go to war we only take the robust, the healthy, the finest types of men. We do not take anybody who is not sound. It is our best men who come back crippled. We never spare any money when it comes to their training, no matter what branch of the service they are attached to, and it is an expensive project to train these young men nowadays. If service in the forces breaks the health of our men or makes them old before their time, it should not be difficult to obtain money with which to compensate them for the loss of health and premature ageing.
I wish that the minister had been able to convince the government to accept the proposals of the Legion, the army, navy and air force and other veterans associations. I think the demands of the various groups were quite reasonable and the government should give them what they ask for.
I do not wish to take the time to go into any of the cases from my own constituency, as I feel this might not be the correct time and place to do so. However, I can speak to the minister about these cases at any time.
There are one or two things to which I hope the committee will give consideration and these have been repeated by the hon. member who preceded me. I am thinking particularly of the imperial veterans who are required to live in this country for 20 years in order to qualify for veterans allowance. If such a veteran were to die two days short of the 20 years his widow cannot qualify. I feel the minister should have the power to review
War Veterans Allowance Act cases of this kind and that perhaps the requirements of 20 years' residence could be reduced to 15 years' residence. Then there is the case of the veteran who is in poor health and has been given advice to go to a southern climate. He loses his pension while he is away. We allow judges and civil servants to go to the sunny south in search of health or enjoyment without stopping their pensions. Surely we could extend this privilege to the veterans in search of a more suitable climate in order to help them in their search for health. I think the permissive income of married veterans could have been increased a little bit more. No doubt this matter will be thoroughly discussed in the veterans affairs committee. I will not be on the veterans affairs committee this year but I have every confidence that the members of all groups will put up a good fight for the veterans. I should like to say thanks to the minister for the many veterans cases he has helped me to straighten out from time to time. I appeal to the minister to give the veterans all he possibly can. Many of these veterans are buying medicine and drugs that take away a great deal of their pension.

I am not one of those people who believe that the amount of money available from taxation is unlimited. I realize, as I think do most other hon. members, that you cannot keep on raising taxes without dislocating the economy.

speechtext:
I was expecting a remark from that hon. member along that line. I feel that there is just so much money in the hands of the government. They can raise only so much money this year from taxation. If they cannot raise any more in order to increase war veterans allowance, possibly some other department might be able to give up their share to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) so that he could increase the war veterans allowance a little more. Half a loaf, I suppose, is better than none at all.
As I have already said, I am glad to see that the war veterans allowance has been increased to a certain extent. The Legion, of course, has put in this request from time to time. I think that most people on this side of the house are in agreement with the Legion's request. I see that they have applied for an increase in the monthly rate for the single man. As the Legion has requested, it has been increased to $60. The ceiling of total annual income is raised only to $840 instead of $1,200. In the case of the married man I see the allowance has been raised from $90 to $108 which is somewhat short of the $120 a month that was suggested by the Legion. I think the biggest discrepancy here is the fact that the Legion recommended that the maximum total annual income be $2,000 and the government at this time was apparently able to raise it only to $1,440. It is to be hoped that, if not now, then in the not too distant future, the government will be able to find the money to follow out the recommendations of the Legion. I think that hon. members would agree that the recommendations of the Legion are by no means unreasonable. The people who compose the executive of the Canadian Legion are highly responsible people, and they have not made those recommendations without having given careful consideration to all the facts concerned.
I should just like to say that I think the redefinition of the expression "casual earnings" which was altered last year has certainly helped those on war veterans allowance a great deal. It is much more elastic than the interpretation used to be.
To get back to the point I mentioned earlier, and the one I should like to make, may I say this. If the ceiling of permissive income was raised to the extent requested by the Legion, undoubtedly it would cost the government a lot more money, and this money would have to be found somewhere. I should just like to make this suggestion. It seems to me that there are several other departments of government that might very well give up some of the moneys that have been allocated to them. For instance, I might mention the Department of Public Works. All over


Canada and abroad there are certain large and fancy government buildings going up, particularly in Ottawa. Inasmuch as we are a growing nation and are becoming a prominent nation, I am not saying that Canada should not have nice government buildings. I think we should. It is a matter of national pride and abroad it may well be a matter of national prestige. But as long as there are citizens such as those who are receiving war veterans allowance in only small amounts, until those people who deserve it have their standard of living raised a little bit more than it has been raised by this bill, I think we could forgo some of the fancy buildings in Ottawa and possibly abroad. I refer to the proposed embassy at Rome and the building going up in Washington. That construction is not going to relieve any unemployment in Canada. I think maybe some of the fancy buildings going up here in Ottawa might either be postponed or might have some of the frills cut down. Some of these buildings look very much like Babylonian palaces and they have everything in them but the hanging gardens; and the C.M.H.C. building out here has nearly got them in it too.
It seems to me that it might be possible to cut down a little bit in that regard and maybe on some other matters like the purchase of expensive works of art for the national gallery. I do not suppose anyone would like more than I would to see Canada have a fine collection of works of art in the national gallery. But until such time as these burned-out pensioners are looked after I think we might forgo the purchase of things such as that, temporarily at least. The same thing could be said about other matters. When one goes through the estimates one sees things like cutlery and china-ware for Government House and things like that. I know those are small matters but in my county there is an expression to the effect that "many a mickle makes a muckle". I do not think the minister has yet been able to give us a completely accurate statement as to how much it would cost to increase the war veterans allowance to the extent requested by the Legion. Possibly he will be able to give us that information a little bit later on. I am sure that he will, probably when we get into committee on this bill.
In conclusion, there is one point I should like to make along the same line. In the estimates last year and this year I see provision for many other government buildings that are going to be put up around the country. I do not think we should cut down on the building of public works in regions, as the government tells us, where there is unemployment because the building

of public works certainly is a palliative if not a cure for unemployment. In places where unemployment is acute I do not think we should cut down in any way on public works; but there are certain parts in the country- maybe not too many but there are some- where unemployment is not too acute. I think maybe in those places the building of expensive government buildings at this time might be cut down a little bit, if that money could be turned to helping those who are in receipt of war veterans allowance. I think most hon. members and their constituents would not mind if the construction of a shiny new post office building in their constituencies was delayed for a year or two provided they knew that the money would be used to help the men who are on war veterans allowance. I am quite sure they would not mind doing without new post offices if they thought it would help.
I do not suppose there will be much attention paid, but the minister might be able to convince some of his colleagues in the cabinet that certain necessary but not immediately urgent expenditures of money in other departments might be delayed until such time as war veterans allowances have been increased a little bit more than is done by the present legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support and compliment the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and the government for bringing in Bill No. 164 to raise war veterans allowances. Those of us who have had the pleasure of dealing with the Minister of Veterans Affairs with respect to various veterans problems cannot help but be impressed with his genuine and sympathetic attitude towards our war veterans. To his predecessors belongs a great deal of the credit for having compiled the veterans charter that we have today. To the present Minister of Veterans Affairs there also goes a great deal of credit for the continuous improvement of the charter since his appointment as head of that department. Whatever bouquets we have for the present minister, may I say that I think they are equally well deserved by his parliamentary assistant and the officials generally throughout the department.
Those of us who served on the veterans affairs committee last year were very disappointed that no increase in war veterans allowances was made during the last session. However, I believe the minister and the government were left in no doubt whatever as to where we stood on the matter. While we would have liked immediate action on our request at the last session, we are very glad that the necessary legislation is now before us. I am glad not only because our
War Veterans Allowance Act older veterans need assistance but also because the introduction of the legislation shows that we do not have to wait for an election year to get some action from the government.
Some disappointment has been expressed that the proposed amendments do not go as far as requested by the Canadian Legion. While I give the Legion full credit for presenting an excellent brief on the subject of war veterans allowances, I am also inclined to give the minister a great deal of credit for having seriously studied the whole question before he brought in the bill. I am glad that he has gone a long way to meet the Legion's request for an increase in the basic rates. A 20 per cent increase is a very good one and is a long step in the right direction. If we cannot get all that the Legion brief asked, then I am happier with an increase in the basic rates than I would have been if they had been left as they were and there had been increases in the permissible income ceilings. I am happy about this because I am convinced that what we are offered in the bill is a far better deal for our needy veterans.
The permissible income ceiling does not mean very much to many of our ageing veterans who are in no position to obtain employment. They will be the first to realize, I am sure, that a bird in the hand is always better than two in the bush. However, I am sure that the whole matter of the permissive income ceilings will be thoroughly aired in the veterans affairs committee. Then there is the question of the supplementary assistance fund. The minister has indicated that the rules governing supplementary allowances are to be revised and made more generous. I believe this will have the effect of giving many needy veterans and widows incomes of $70 per month if single and $120 per month if married. We hope to hear more about the supplementary allowances in the committee. Allowances on this scale are, I believe, well in line with what has been requested by the Canadian Legion.
Then we have the clause on casual earnings which will be of real help to some veterans and widows of veterans. We will have a more detailed examination of the bill in the committee and therefore I do not intend to take up the time of the house with further comment at this time. However, I could not allow this opportunity to pass without letting the government and the minister know that I consider the bill another real step forward in veterans legislation. It is by progressive steps such as this one that we have achieved the fine veterans charter we have today. Of course I realize it is far from perfect but I believe it to be well worthy of our support. Therefore I say to the minister, "So far, so

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two telegrams have reached me over the week end. One is from the secretary of the Canadian Legion branch at Hudson Bay, Saskatchewan, urging that I support the Legion's brief when Bill 164 is before the house. The other is from the zone commander of zone No. 3 in Saskatchewan, also urging that the Legion's proposals be given favourable consideration by the house. It has been suggested that Canada's legislation for veterans is the best in the world. I am afraid it would not be easy for us to convince the veterans who are dependent on the provisions we have made that what we have provided is the best that Canada can offer. During the war the then minister of finance emphasized again and again that what was physically possible would be made financially possible. Never once during the years from 1939 to 1945 did any minister of the government say that he did not have enough money to carry on his job.
I am sorry that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), who had the responsibility of introducing the legislation, made it appear as if he thought it was adequate.
I wish that one of the older members of the cabinet who sits on the treasury board had taken on the responsibility and presented the arguments. To suggest that the Canadian economy would not stand an extra $13 million to meet the requests of the Canadian Legion is absurd. Last year the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) was given something like $2 billion to carry on his job. Press reports would indicate that he is approximately $175 million short of having spent all that we voted him. If he had spent the full amount there would not be any criticism, and I submit that we should at least go as far as the Legion has suggested. Ways and means certainly could be found to provide an additional $13 million.
A large part of the area where I live was settled by veterans at the end of the first world war. The names they gave to their school districts suggest places that are well known to us-Somme, Blighty, Veterans, Souchez and Vimy. It is very difficult for members of the house to appreciate the sort of assignment these veterans undertook when they took over 160 acres of land in the bush country at a price of $10 and proceeded to clear the land and bring it under cultivation. They had just nicely made a start when the depression came upon them, and for many years now life has been very difficult. I feel


it is unfair for the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) to suggest that $840 is a reasonable amount of income for a single person, and it is equally unfair to suggest that $1,440 is the maximum amount which a wealthy country like Canada can provide for married veterans.
The legislation before us, in addition to making provision for the veterans, also provides for certain salary increases. Section 6 provides that the salary of the chairman will be increased to $11,000 from $10,000, while the salaries of the other board members will be increased from $8,500 to $9,500. I am sure that those salaries will not put the commission members out of line with salaries being paid to men in other branches of government doing comparable work. However, the fact that the government considers these people doing responsible work require an additional $1,000 a year surely makes it impossible to suggest that $840 is the maximum amount a single person should have or that a married man should have $1,440 as a maximum.
The last copy of The Legionary which has reached our desks mentions that at last war veterans allowances were being increased. There is also this important heading "Good, but not Enough". I am sure that the considered opinions that have been presented by members in all sections of the house should result in the committee coming back with a recommendation to parliament that the maximum for single men be at least $1,200 and for married men $2,000. I believe that is the very least we could suggest as the maximum total annual income, including allowances.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
We
have had a large number of eloquent and moving pleas in this debate on behalf of the recipients of war veterans allowances, and those who are potential recipients. I agree completely with the statements which have been made concerning the hardships endured in the first war by men who are now recipients of war veterans allowances. I agree also with the remarks made about the great service they rendered to this country and to the cause of freedom throughout the world. It is significant that no one, during this debate or any previous debate on this subject that I have heard, has ever questioned the service or the value of the service these men have rendered. Since that is so, it seems to me that in this parliament we should be prepared to take the most generous view possible of the treatment these old soldiers should receive.
I am sorry to say that I do not believe that has always been the attitude of the government. I think there has been altogether too

much of the attitude, well, this might cost $3 million more or $6 million more per year, and therefore we cannot do it; we will wait until a few more of these people die, and then we might be able to increase the payments. I do not think the Canadian people or the members of this house, as representatives of them, really subscribe to that point of view. I feel quite convinced that, given a free rein, the members of this house would be overwhelmingly in favour of granting war veterans allowance recipients the full amount recommended by the Legion and other veterans organizations during the past year or two.
I know that a large number of the recipients of war veterans allowances would be gratified by the increases provided in this particular bill. I was glad to see those increases of $10 per month for single men and $18 per month for married men. Many of us on this side of the house for years have been urging the government to increase the amount of these allowances. Last year in the veterans committee we made very strong pleas that the amount be raised to $60 per month for single men and $120 per month for married men. The fact that the government has met the recommendation for single men and has gone some distance towards meeting the recommendation for married men is naturally gratifying. I am glad to see that some of the government members who were on that veterans committee last year are expressing satisfaction over the increases that have been made.
I am only sorry that they did not express the same ideas last year, and join with the other members on that committee in attempting to force the government to introduce increases at that time. Then these veterans who are now going to have these increases would have had them a year ago instead of getting them this coming summer. It is all very well for members to say at this stage they are glad to see these increases, but if those members supporting the Liberal government had really put the pressure on last year or the year before these increases might have been in effect long before this.
The great defect, so far as this piece of legislation is concerned, is that there has been no real increase made in the amount of income which the recipients of war veterans allowance can receive, apart from the allowance itself. There has been a great deal of talk here about the increase from $720 per year to $840 per year in the income of single men. All that is, however, is an increase of $10 per month which has been made in the allowance, raising the allowance from $50 to $60 per month. The single man is still in a position where he cannot secure
War Veterans Allowance Act more than $10 per month above the allowance. In other words, there has been no increase in allowable income above the allowance at all. The same situation holds true of the married men, except they can have an income of $12 per month above the allowance instead of the $10 per month as it was before. There has been an increase there of $2 per month, but not enough to amount to anything.
It has always been very difficult for me to understand why the government has so consistently refused to increase the amount of allowable income for the recipients of war veterans allowances. This has been the case for the last ten years, and pleas have been made to increase the allowable income to the level of income tax exemptions. It does not seem reasonable that the income tax exemption level of $1,000 for single men and $2,000 for married men should be too high an allowance for the recipients of war veterans allowances to reach before anything is taken off their allowance. I would hope when this matter is considered in the committee that the majority of the committee would be prepared to recommend that the whole matter be reconsidered, and that the amount of allowable income be increased to at least the income tax exemption levels, as has been recommended so frequently for such a long period of time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for just a few moments to give further support to the requests being made that the committee to which this bill will be referred give serious consideration to the original proposals of the Canadian Legion so far as the War Veterans Allowance Act is concerned.
It is not often that we in this house, since we both listen to and make a great many speeches, will admit that we are moved by the utterances we hear from other members; but I am sure all of us have been deeply moved by the appeals that have been made from various quarters of this house. I think we all feel that way about the speech made today by my friend and neighbour, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and also in connection with the very strong and moving speech made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes).
I express the hope that the appeals made by these hon. members, as well as the appeal made on Friday by my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and others in this group, will be listened to by the government and by those who will deal with this legislation when it gets to the special committee on veterans affairs.

War Veterans Allowance Act
It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is significance which should be noted in the many telegrams that hon. members are now receiving. I know the attitude of some on the government side is to say that it is easy for hon. members to produce telegrams. We are getting them all the time. But I suggest there is particular significance in the fact that now that the terms of Bill No. 164 are out, the Legion branches across the country are wiring their members expressing their view that the original requests of the Legion should even yet be met in full.
I too have received telegrams in connection with this matter. I think of a particular one 1 have on my desk which comes from Mr. P. Johnson, the president, and Mr. Thomas C. Wetton, the secretary of the Imperial division of the Canadian Legion in Winnipeg, a branch of which I have the very high honour to be an honorary member. This branch, like others, is urging that we give our utmost support, in connection with the consideration of Bill No. 164, to the full implementation of the Legion's original recommendations. And all of us know what is meant by that request.
Therefore I hope, Mr. Speaker, that when this bill goes to the committee it will be considered in an open-minded fashion, and that the possibility of amending it will be regarded by the members as very real. I say that despite the words used the other night by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), when he said, as reported at page 1755 of Hansard:
I would not want to leave any shadow of a suggestion that I think there will be any substantial change by way of raising the ceilings on permissive income in the veterans affairs committee.
I was sorry to hear that statement, Mr. Speaker. Surely there is no point in setting up a committee if one is going to attempt to close the door on it before it even goes into session. I was glad to hear another Liberal member, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), suggest this afternoon that it will be possible in that committee to consider all the aspects of this bill, and I hope that will be done not just in an academic fashion but in the light of the appeals that are being made, and in the light of the fact that it is possible for that committee to recommend to the government or back to the house that further improvements be made in this legislation at this time.
Everyone knows what it is that requires improvement. In the main, there are three points: first, the question of the ceiling on permissive income; second, the matter of the definition regarding imperial veterans or


widows of imperial veterans; third, the question of the United Kingdom not yet being regarded as a theatre of war for purposes of world war I.
With regard to the ceiling, Mr. Speaker, an unfortunate argument has been made both by the hon. member for Vancouver South and by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona in suggesting that if a choice had to be made between the raising of the ceiling on permissive income and an increase in the amount of the allowance, the choice would be for the increase in the amount of the allowance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver South says "hear, hear". He repeats his argument. Is he so naive as to think that it has to be either/or? The Legion did not ask for one or the other. No one is now suggesting that instead of the increase in the allowance there should be a raising of the permissive ceiling. What we are asking for is that the original, responsible, shall I say conservative requests of the Canadian Legion be met in full, both with respect to the amount of the allowance and the ceiling on permissive income.
As I said when I spoke on this matter at the resolution stage, Mr. Speaker, I think it is a bit of a hoax to spread the idea that this bill provides an increase in the other income allowed a burnt-out pensioner. It is true that the ceiling on the total income is raised, but only to the extent that the allowance has been raised, so when you look at the amount of other income that one is permitted to earn under the terms of the act, you see there has been no increase provided in the case of the single veteran, and only $2 a month in the case of the married veteran.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the Legion branches across this country and the dominion command in so far as its views are expressed in the current issue of The Legionary are fully justified in saying at this time that this is not good enough. I support as strongly as I can the plea, the earnest request that the committee, when it deals with this bill, recommend that the ceilings on permissive income be raised to the figures proposed by the Legion, namely $1,200 a year for single veterans and $2,000 a year for married veterans. These figures would also solve the problem that arises in connection with old age security when a veteran reaches 70.
On the other two points, I should like simply to repeat what I have already mentioned. I feel that there should be a change in regard to the status of imperial veterans,

and particularly in the case of the widows of imperial veterans. As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich pointed out, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Mac-Dougall) completely missed the point the other night; the widow of the imperial veteran who was not in Canada for the full 20 years has no hope of ever getting an allowance no matter how long she lives, even though she herself may have been born in this country. It does seem to me that there is room for improvement there; that decency, common sense and common fair play call for a change in that respect.
Likewise, Mr. Speaker, now that we are this far away from the struggle of 1914-1918, it does seem to me that we should accord to the veterans of world war I who went overseas, and who were perfectly willing to go to France but did not get beyond the United Kingdom, the same treatment that we accord to veterans of world war II. It is high time the United Kingdom was declared a theatre of war in world war I for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act with respect both to veterans themselves and to widows of veterans who should be allowed to qualify under the provisions of the act.
My purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, is to plead as strongly as I can that these three points, among others, be dealt with satisfactorily by the committee to which this bill is to be referred.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
I have listened to this debate with great interest, and I notice that a number of hon. members have welcomed the terms of the bill on the principle that half a loaf is better than no bread at all. Other hon. members have frankly and strongly criticized the government, I think rightly, for bringing forth a half measure and because they are continuing the practice of dealing with veterans, especially those of world war I, in a piecemeal manner. As time goes on and the pressure from the Canadian Legion and individual citizens of this country can be held out against no longer, they	decide	to	make concessions. Isubmit that	is	not	the	way in which this
problem should be approached.
It is generally recognized by the Canadian people that we	owe	to	the veterans of bothworld wars,	in	fact	of	all wars, a debt not
only of gratitude but to see that they end their days with a reasonable standard of living. It is a medical fact, as has been so ably pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, that because of their service and the hardship they have suffered their ability to earn a livelihood has been greatly reduced, as well as their ability to save for a rainy day.
War Veterans Allowance Act
In addition to that, it is generally acknowledged that because of their service these veterans have pre-aged by ten years. That was the principle underlying this legislation when it was brought in. In effect the war veterans allowance is an old age pension which is given to a war veteran ten years earlier than the average citizen because he has been aged prematurely by the hardships he experienced while on active service.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext: If you applied your argument would it not be true that we would have to reduce the war veterans allowance to $40 per month?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I do not think that necessarily follows. It is true that the war veterans allowance is greater than the old age pension, but it does not necessarily follow that it would automatically have to be reduced. I appreciate the point brought up by the hon. member, but I have said already that in addition to being pre-aged by ten years it is also recognized that the earning capacity of these men during their productive years has been reduced, and their period of earning shortened by ten years. Incidentally, their life expectancy is not as great as that of other citizens.
There are three reasons which might be advanced as to why they should receive the old age pension at a slightly higher level than the average person. They have not been able to earn so long; they will probably die off sooner, and their earning capacity during their productive years is not as great. But that is by the way.
What does not make logic to me is the penny-pinching attitude which the minister has expressed on behalf of the government in regard to permissible earnings over and above the war veterans allowance. In the case of the single veteran the permissible earnings have not been increased at all, and in the case of the married veteran they have been increased by $2 per month.
I realize that if the ceiling on total permissible income were increased it would mean that veterans not now receiving the full veterans allowance would have their allowances increased. It would mean also that classes of veterans who now do not qualify for the allowance would qualify. But I do not think either group would be large, and even if it were I do not think that is a point to be considered. At the present time we are expecting the single veteran to live decently on $2.30 per day, and we expect a veteran and his wife to eke out a living on $3.90 per day. All the Canadian Legion is asking, and all many hon. members are pressing for, is that in the case of the married veteran the

War Veterans Allowance Act ceiling on total earnings be raised to $2,000 so that he and his wife would have $5.48 per day on which to live. I think it will be agreed that that would not provide an extravagant standard of living for two people, with the cost of living what it is at the present time.
It should be remembered that the time is running out during which we will have the privilege of paying our debt to the veterans of the first world war. The youngest soldier in the first world war is now 55 years of age, which means that in 15 years every veteran of the first world war will be at least 70 years of age. As I understand it, in the next 15 years in most cases the war veterans allowance will be decreased by the amount of the universal old age pension which a veteran would receive on reaching 70 years of age. The result will be that in 15 years the war veterans allowance for all veterans of the first world war will be reduced by $40 per month, a considerable reduction in the cost of this program to the department without increasing in any way the amount paid out by the government for universal old age pensions.
That is all I wish to say on this matter, except to indicate that I also have received telegrams from various Legion branches. I should like to read one which I received from the Prince Edward Island provincial command of the Canadian Legion, reading as follows:
Prince Edward Island command Canadian Legion urge you support the Canadian Legion recommendation that war veterans allowances be increased to $80 per month for single and $120 for married men and the ceiling for permissible earnings be $1,200 for single men and $2,000 for married.
I heartily support that recommendation of the Canadian Legion, because I think it is reasonable. I see no fault as far as the other amendments are concerned. Obviously it is a needed correction to amend the act so that parents will include adoptive, foster and step-parents. I think that is only justice, and I approve of it most heartily.
