speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is evident from the tenor of the debate that this measure will receive the unanimous support of the house, but I would be rather reluctant to feel that the government should take our unanimity as an indication that we are satisfied with the measure, and that the government has gone as far at this time as the Canadian Legion and others interested in the welfare of the veterans would have them go.
Like many hon. members I have received communications from Legion members in my own constituency. This morning I received


a wire from Ron Shawcross, president of the Legion branch in Regina which has 1,700 members, expressing their dissatisfaction with this measure. In his wire to me Mr. Shawcross points out:
You will agree impossible for single man to live on $840 and married man on $1,440 per year.
I think that wire sums up the attitude of the Legion members in my constituency. I recall that the hon. member for Vancouver South indicated the other day that the veterans in his constituency were not as concerned about allowable income as they were about the cash increase itself. I would suggest the veterans in my constituency are definitely concerned about allowable income, and they feel that it should be set at the figure outlined by the dominion command of the Canadian Legion. This proposal has been supported by a great many hon. members who have spoken in this debate.
It seems rather strange, as the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) pointed out, that in the same bill which calls for increases for the veterans there is a provision for an increase in the salaries of the chairman of the board and the board members. Apparently the government feels that $11,000 is now necessary as recompense for the chairman of the board. It does seem a little inconsistent that the government should feel $840 is a sufficient amount of money to maintain a single veteran, and $1,440 is sufficient to maintain a married veteran.
I rise at this time simply because of some of the statements made by supporters of the government, who seem to take great pride in the record of the government concerning veterans legislation. As pointed out by many hon. members in other groups, we have a good record in veterans legislation in many respects. However, I feel it is not proper procedure to use that as an excuse for holding back on benefits at this time. If the legislation is as good as government supporters are so fond of telling us, the government should make it better still. There seems to be no reason whatsoever to take the attitude that we are satisfied with the legislation and have no intention of improving it.
In line with the recommendations made by the Regina branch of the Canadian Legion, I want to urge the government to give further consideration to this matter. I hope that when the bill goes to the committee it will bring back recommendations calling for improvements in this bill in line with the recommendations set forth by the Canadian Legion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
I
rise to take part briefly in this debate simply in order to add my voice to those of the other

members who have pleaded in such a fair manner on behalf of those who receive the war veterans allowance.
I am certain the minister and his parliamentary assistant must have been moved when they listened this afternoon to the fine speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. There are still a few members in this house who went through the first war; and while it was quite a long time ago any member who went through the battles known as Passchendaele, Ploegsteert or Vimy Ridge, or who fought down on the Somme, or who had anything to do with Sugar trench or Regina trench, can quite understand and appreciate why the belief has grown up that the experiences and ordeals these men went through have shortened their lives by at least ten years. I say that despite what the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Fairey) may say to the contrary.
These benefits are of great importance to these men, as the hon. member who preceded me has pointed out. The number of men who receive these benefits and who have continued to receive them is decreasing year by year. The minister knows only too well that it will be many years before the War Veterans Allowance Act will be again before the house for amendment so the allowance may be increased or the ceiling raised. I therefore urge the minister to take advantage of this opportunity and at least recommend changes that will comply with the recommendations received from the Canadian Legion.
Other hon. members have pointed out the discrimination as far as the old age pension being paid to those who receive war veterans allowance is' concerned. We all recall that when this great piece of legislation was introduced whereby all Canadians reaching the age of 70 would receive a security pension of $40 a month it was applauded and approved by all members in the house. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the war veteran who receives a burnt-out pension or the war veterans allowance is discriminated against because, as you well know, when he reaches the age of 70 he receives the old age pension and security cheque of $40 a month but his war veterans allowance is accordingly decreased by $40 a month.
I am sure the minister must have received many complaints, and must know what happens when the veteran who is struggling so hard to get along earns a little more money than is allowed him under the ceiling. The veteran is required to fill out a long yellow legal form which tells everything about him and which is gone over with a magnifying 50433-1134
War Veterans Allowance Act glass. If the form reveals that he has exceeded the very low ceiling he is notified in due course that his allowance has been reduced accordingly. The minister must know from long experience the length of time required for the veteran to get his allowance back to the old rate.
I especially plead with the minister to raise the ceiling to encourage the veteran to earn what he can. The veteran has found from bitter experience, in seeing what has happened to his chums and neighbours, that once he goes over the ceiling his allowance is reduced.
I do not want to point out the difference between the benefits received by the veterans of the first war and those of the second war. I was glad to see that the veterans of the second war received what they did, because I feel they deserved it. However, the benefits that were given to the veterans of the first war were very meagre in comparison with the benefits given to the veterans of the second war.
The minister knows the attitude of the Legion. As one hon. member said today, many of the hon. members are receiving telegrams from their Legion branches throughout their ridings urging them to support the demands made by the Legion. I would simply conclude by saying that I do hope the minister on this occasion and even at this late date will consider amendments which will provide for the full recommendations made by the Canadian Legion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has carried on for two days and a great deal of argument has been presented on behalf of the veterans, but there are certain new facts which have arisen today and I think the address made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre brought out some principles which have not been presented previously.
The hon. member spoke of the fact that these veterans not only served in the first war but went through a period of depression which lasted for ten years. He pointed out the difference in the treatment of the veterans of the first and second wars. I honour those veterans of the second war, but I feel that the veterans of the first war did not have the opportunities which were afforded second world war veterans. I remember very well the matter of getting the gratuity, and allowances, and that sort of thing. But educational opportunities were given after the second war, and a great deal of other assistance was given.
Not only was that fact apparent, but these men came through a period of ten years when they had no opportunity to hold a job, to

War Veterans Allowance Act build up a business, or to rehabilitate themselves in life. When we consider veterans of the first war that is something we should seriously take into consideration. The matter of ageing ten years, in addition to their proper age, is something that cannot be questioned. There is no doubt on that matter.
With regard to this matter I have received telegrams and letters, the same as every other hon. member in this house. However, there was one letter which impressed me particularly and I am going to quote parts of it. I shall send the letter over to the minister for verification, because this man has presented his arguments most clearly. He states his argument in this way. He begins by saying that their Legion branch was greatly disappointed. Then he starts to point out his personal condition:
A single person has to pay $15 per week for board, on a 28 day month. He is only allowed $60 per month.
That is a single veteran, so his $60 is entirely taken up in board allowance. He continues:
For a married person-
And he cites his own personal condition.
-I find that it takes me $100 a month for my groceries, milk and meat, and we live very plain at that. What is a person going to do with the other $8?
But then he goes on and tells me how he is paying in to the superannuation fund and that he will get out just his $1,440 per year. But this is the telling paragraph in his letter:
My family doctor has been telling my wife for years that I am really ten years older than X am due to war services, but my birth certificate only gives me 60 years instead of 70, so the old age security is out.
This is the impressive part of this letter. I know this man to be a good man. I know him to be a man who works, and who was a good soldier all the way through. I want to bring this one sentence to the attention of the house. After saying that old age security is out he goes on to say this:
I won't be around in another ten years, can't afford to quit my job, so will have to work as long as possible.
I believe what this man says. He is a man who is aged prematurely, and he has no recourse but to work as long as he possibly can stagger along and keep going, because he is not going to receive from war veterans allowance sufficient to let him lead the life he should lead, and which he is entitled to lead by virtue of his service.
There is no doubt about the ten years' premature ageing. I think of those veterans of the first war who did not participate in a war of movement, but who spent that four years in mud in the trenches. The situation


was entirely different. They aged. It was difficult to rehabilitate them when they came back. Now with the high cost of living, in times such as these, no man can support a wife adequately on this allowance. It is just foolish to think that two old people can get along on $1,440 a year.
As to the arguments that have been placed before us about the government having acted in a wonderful way, let me say that we owe this consideration to these people. This matter has been brought before the government time and time again. The Canadian Legion is not a pressure group; it is a group of responsible citizens. These people know the condition of the veterans better than any other group of people in Canada.
I was impressed by the address given by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. There is no man in this house who has a better knowledge of the condition of these veterans. Finding this hon. member pleading for the men who served under him, knowing full well their condition, I could not hesitate to say to this house: Let us try to raise this ceiling; let us do something about it. There is no doubt that these men have earned it, that they need it, and that they should have the means of enjoying a decent way of living. That is all I have to say, because other arguments have been presented. I plead with hon. members that some further assistance be given to these people.
Before I sit down there is one thing I want to say to the minister. I find a great deal of difficulty in explaining to soldiers that veterans of the first war are not eligible for war veterans allowance if they served only in England. These old fellows-and I say "old fellows" in a kindly way-cannot understand why they are not eligible when veterans of the second war are eligible. This matter should receive a great deal of consideration. I would suggest to the minister that this matter be more clearly placed before his colleagues, and that consideration be given to extending the benefits to these people. In many cases they performed excellent service. Many of them were unfit. It was not their fault that they did not get across the channel. As I say, I find a great deal of difficulty in trying to explain to these men why they are not eligible for war veterans allowance.
I appeal to the minister to reconsider this whole bill. I appeal to him to realize that the Canadian Legion is a responsible group of citizens, and that we have telegrams and letters coming in from old-timers across the country. I particularly plead for those of the first war, because they are in that age group. I urge that something further be done

to extend this bill. It is not too late. If it were done it would give a great deal of satisfaction to these people who are trying to get along on a meagre salary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not allow this opportunity to go by without saying something on this motion, which is to refer Bill No. 164 to the committee.
I just want to say that across our country from Cape Breton right to Vancouver we have veterans in this category. I submit that there is no class of Canadian citizens to whom we as Canadians owe a greater debt. I feel sure everyone recognizes, as has been indicated by those who have spoken previously in this debate, that these veterans were prepared to go out for their country and make their contribution, whatever it should be, in the way of safeguarding the welfare of every Canadian citizen as well as the welfare and peace of the world. I therefore want to join with those members in this house who have stated that this measure is not good enough.
I agree with the Canadian Legion, which has indicated that it is a welcome move in the right direction; but I for one want to voice my opinion that it is not good enough under present conditions. I do not think we in this house are justified in comparing it with any other legislation in any other country. I believe we have our own specific responsibility, and that we should make the legislation the best we can do for those veterans of the first great war.
In my own constituency I have veterans in this class whom I see from time to time. In my own little home town I have a number of them, and I see them trying to supplement their income under the war veterans allowance by jobs such as taking the mail to the train and bringing it back, casual labour with the pick and shovel, and many other kinds of jobs, sometimes when they are not fit to do that type of work. They do this simply because they are not in receipt of a proper income which would give them a decent standard of living.
I know it is difficult to translate the needs of these people in order to find what would give them a decent standard of living; but I have made some attempt to find out what would be a reasonable income which would guarantee these veterans a decent standard of living. I am quite sure that no member of this house will gainsay my statement when I say they should at least have a decent standard of living.
I want to put before you, Mr. Speaker, and before the house the findings of the united automobile workers' survey as set out in the Guardian, and they have taken this survey
War Veterans Allowance Act from the standards of the United States department of labour. This is not a mere subsistence level budget, but a very modest budget. I think one can say that one should not expect any Canadian to live on less than is provided in this type of budget.
The costs in this survey are those which prevailed in Windsor, Ontario, as of January 31, 1954. The survey takes a family of four, the father being 38 years of age, the mother 36, with a son of 15 and a daughter 13. All members will recognize, and quite rightly, that by and large war veterans will be much older, but I submit this is a comparable basis. I might digress to say that in my constituency I have such war veterans in receipt of war veterans allowance who still have dependents, although their age is somewhat greater.
In this survey there are no other dependents. The family has three bedroom rented living accommodation, and the home is within reasonable commuting distance of work. All cooking, laundry and preparation of lunches are done at home. Five per cent of meals are eaten away from home, leaving 95 per cent prepared and eaten in the home. The budget only allows a few meat servings each week, with chicken or turkey on New Year's or Christmas days. It restricts the choice of food and the choice of entertainment for these people. The total amount for recreation for the family of four is set at $91 a year. This family has no car. In order to provide for their modest budget there must be an income of $3,746.18 a year. Where the home is owned but there is no car the family would need $3,431.88. When the family are buying their home and also have no car they would need $3,971.88. In no case do these figures allow for any income tax.
There, sir, are the figures established after a careful survey with respect to the cost of living in Canada for a family of four. When one considers this modest budget one can hardly say that the proposed increases in war veterans allowance are at all adequate. As a matter of fact I think they are shameful. In terms of the 1945 dollar, the dollar given to the veteran today is worth only about 50 per cent of what it was then. In my opinion the demands of the Canadian Legion, as outlined in The Legionary of March, 1955, are more than reasonable. It may possibly be that the veterans have become accustomed to the failure of the government in the past to assume its responsibility to provide adequate pensions for them.
I want to bring one other matter to the attention of the house with reference to the proposed increase in the income of the single veteran. It is proposed that the maximum
1786	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act allowable income will be $840. To take but one example, a veteran who is 69 years of age will receive a maximum of $70 a month. When he becomes 70, within a year, he will still have a monthly income maximum of $70, but his war veterans allowance will be decreased by the amount of $40 representing the old age pension. In that case he will only get $30 by way of war veterans allowance.
As far as I am concerned the increase in war veterans allowance granted to veterans of the first great war is niggardly. With a properly organized Canada, having in mind the potential production of this country and having in mind that this matter is the responsibility of parliament, the government should listen to the views of those on this side of the house and grant a decent and adequate pension for these people who were ready to go and give their best for their country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is perhaps the most favourable time for those veterans and other interested members who will not be members of the committee to make their thoughts known, I wish to state briefly that these increases of approximately 20 per cent do not in my opinion go far enough.
It was in my home city in the late 1920's, shortly after the formation of the Canadian Legion that, I believe, the principle already mentioned in this debate, that a veteran with front-line service had aged prematurely by ten years, was laid down. To my knowledge this principle has never been disputed and is still acknowledged today. I have had some personal connection with benevolent work, mainly through the distribution of the proceeds of the various poppy campaigns, and I think I can state with some authority that the incentive to veterans to work will not be increased greatly with a 20 per cent increase in the allowance.
I am pleased to note that some amendments are to be made with respect to the veterans assistance fund, which is of course most necessary. But those of us who have had something to do with the plight of veterans in our respective communities should recognize that the incentive for the veteran to find full or part-time employment will not be strengthened unless the allowances are raised to the amounts requested by the Canadian Legion.
There is one other matter I should like to mention. In the seaport towns there are a great many merchant seamen who rendered good service at sea during the war and who aged in the same way other veterans did, but they have not been given the same


benefits as other veterans. The former minister of veterans affairs knows my feelings as far as the merchant seamen are concerned, and I should like the new minister to understand that I am still interested in them. I grant that the searching of records to establish the service of these men presents quite a problem, but when need is a factor surely some allowance could be made.
I have my share of telegrams here. We have our share of veterans in New Brunswick. There is nothing more I should like to add now except to endorse the words of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), who has always taken a sincere interest in these matters, and to refer again to the headline of the editorial in the last issue of The Legionary which so aptly described the present situation in this way, that the war veterans allowance increases are perhaps good but they are not good enough.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to add my voice to the voices of other hon. members who have welcomed this legislation but who, at the same time, have pointed out that the government should have accepted in full the recommendation made to it by the Canadian Legion. This legislation, which constitutes some improvement, has been long overdue. I have often remarked that the government's attitude toward the recipients of war veterans allowances places those men in a worse position than almost any other group of Canadians.
I believe that the recommendation of the Canadian Legion requesting that war veterans allowances for single persons be increased to $60, and for married persons to $120, was reasonable and should have been granted in full. We welcome, of course, all the increases. We are particularly pleased with the increase to the single veteran, which is in line with the recommendation of the Canadian Legion. We regret very much, however, the fact that the government has failed to grant the request of the Canadian Legion that the allowance for a married veteran should be increased to $120 per month.
Members have pointed out that these veterans are men who sacrificed their health in the first great war, fighting for democracy. The very least that Canada, through its government, should do for these veterans now is to provide them with a minimum standard of living, at least somewhat in keeping with Canadian standards. I suggest with great deference that the action taken by the government falls far short of providing these veterans with the standard of living that should be granted in Canada in 1955.

The Canadian Legion asked that the allowable income for a single veteran be increased to $1,200, and for a married veteran to $2,000. In this respect the government's action falls far short of the request of the Legion, and far short of anything that is adequate. The total allowance now for a single veteran is $840. This is a great deal short of the Legion's request for $1,200. Similarly the allowable income of $1,440 for a married veteran is a great deal short of the Legion request that the allowable income be increased to $2,000.
There is another part of this bill that provides for an increase to members of the board. The chairman's salary is to be increased from $10,000 per year to $11,000 per year. The salary of each of the members will be increased from $8,500 to $9,500. I do not suppose the Canadian Legion would take objection to such increases, but I think they would be much easier for the Legion and others to accept had the government granted the Legion's requests in full. I cannot understand why the war veterans allowance should be decreased when a recipient of that allowance reaches the age of 70 and becomes entitled to the old age security pension. I do not understand why the government should place members receiving the war veterans allowance in a different category from any other group of Canadians.
Why should persons receiving war veterans allowances be singled out for a reduction in their income, and consequently singled out as the one group of Canadians who are not given the full increase of $40 per month in income on reaching the age of 70? As has already been pointed out, a single veteran receiving the maximum allowance of $60 per month, without any other outside income, has his war veterans allowance decreased from $60 to $30 when he reaches 70 and becomes eligible for old age security. I want to support other members who have suggested that the government should reconsider the provisions of this bill in the light of the requests of the Canadian Legion, and that they grant all the requests of the Canadian Legion as being reasonable and responsible requests that should be met in full.

speechtext:
I want to take this opportunity of indicating briefly the reason for my support of those who have said this legislation does not go far enough. At the beginning I should like to make it clear that I am in the same position as many of my colleagues, namely that as veterans of the second world war we want to take this opportunity of expressing our appreciation of the work done and the contributions to national security and national welfare made by those older veterans who served in the
War Veterans Allowance Act first war. We are under obligation to them in that not only did they take part in a war which, in so far as long periods in the trenches under arduous conditions were concerned, in some ways imposed greater hardship, I imagine, than the second world war; but also since their return they have shown their public spirit by forming the organization which has grown into that great body, the Canadian Legion.
All veterans, but particularly those who served in the second war, owe a great deal to the Legion. Had it not been for the Legion during the second war the veterans' rehabilitation and welfare programs would not be anything like as extensive or as complete as they are now. I have the greatest pleasure in expressing commendation of all the work of the Legion; and of course it deserves great praise with respect to this subject of war veterans allowances, and particularly its criticism of the government for not doing what should be done at this time and for having waited so long before doing what it is doing now.
I find it difficult to understand why the government should persist in this attitude correctly described the other evening by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Hark-ness) as "niggling". Why, when they were going to extend the benefits of war veterans allowances, did they not do the whole job? For many of these old veterans it is already too little and too late, so why make it less and later? Certainly no one can be other than appreciative of the fact that there has been some increase in the amount of the allowance itself, but why be niggling about it and leave the maximum permissive income in the same relative position that it was before this increase was granted?
I point out that the Legion does not ask for the elimination of the ceiling on maximum permissible income. They make a very sensible and moderate request, that it be increased to a level at which, heaven knows, even if it were granted no person would live in luxury. A person confined to the limits of the maximum income suggested by the Legion would still live rather close to penury. I do not see why the government should condemn these veterans who deserve so much to living in even less than penury, which they do by the fact they have not accepted the request and changed the relative level of the means test applicable to these allowances.
I agree with the member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) that this is the appropriate time for any of us to express our opinions on this matter, because of the fact that the number of members on the committee is to
1788	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act be limited. I hope, as have other hon. members who have spoken, that the committee and the government will be moved by the speeches that have been made, and I refer particularly to those of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, which I am sure, if viewed impartially, could not have any other effect than to appeal to the common sense as well as the emotions of those who are concerned about this problem. I express the earnest hope that they will carry great weight with the committee and that the government will leave the committee, and that the government members on it will leave themselves, open to receive the requests when they are made there and to accept and act upon them.
I know there is always the problem of financing these things. Any further increase in the amount of the allowance, or any raising of the ceiling on permissive income, would involve expenditures. That is true. But there are many ways in which those expenditures could be met, ways we have suggested here from time to time which would follow as a result of adopting economies that have been proposed in other directions.
I see the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) in his seat at the moment. I am glad he is here, because he comes from British Columbia where the highest proportion of recipients of war veterans allowances live. I hope he will use his influence to have the Legion's request accepted and further amendments made to this bill in committee.
I want to suggest a positive step for his consideration and that of the government, if it is really so hard put to find ways and means of financing any further extension of the legislation. We have suggested a number of economies from time to time. I understand that the minister in a few months will embark upon a trip to Moscow to attend a whaling convention. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that in Moscow we have a most excellent ambassador who speaks Russian, a man of the highest mental calibre and well equipped to understand and speak for Canada on matters such as this. In addition, I am informed that we do not have much of a whaling industry in Canada anyway, and I am certain that the interests of the country would be just as well served by allowing the ambassador who is in Russia to speak for Canada at this convention. Then the minister might donate the expenses which would be saved as a contribution toward making possible an increase in war veterans allowances.

speechtext:
I
appreciate very much this debate and the speeches of hon. members of the opposition. They have been telling us a good deal about the Canadian Legion. We have a branch of the Canadian Legion in Fort William which is second to none, and I respect them very highly for their unselfish service and lots of it.
Of course I do not like to hear somebody suggest that the government have not done anything for the veterans, that they have been neglecting them. I remember that not very long ago the Canadian Legion asked for an increase of 25 per cent, and it was granted. When I think of what this government has done in the way of education for the young veterans who went overseas in the second world war I feel that it ought not to take second place to anybody or anything in its dealings with veterans.
I should like to see certain things done that are not in this bill. I should like to see the permissive income a little higher, as the Canadian Legion requested. But I am not the government. I shall refer to that another time when I think it is my duty to do so. I should like to have seen in this bill pensions for veterans at 60 years of age, without a means test. But this is not the only veterans legislation that is to be brought before the house this year. There is a notice of motion on the order paper dealing with the appointment of a committee, and as long as I am in the house I am going to stand and fight for a pension for the veterans at 60 years of age, without a means test. I think that is only fair. There are veterans in Fort William who are ten years younger than I am, but they would not stand up to

me very long. Why? Because they spent four years in the mud and wet, sometimes with poor meals. I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs will find a way of granting pensions to the veterans at 60 years of age, without a means test.
I am going to support the Minister of Veterans Affairs with respect to this legislation because it is a whole lot better than nothing, and a lot of veterans appreciate it.

speechtext:
Over the week end I had an opportunity to discuss this bill with the officers and some of the members of the Canadian Legion in my riding. I find their reaction rather mixed. In the first place they are grateful for the advantages which this bill offers, and they wanted to make clear in no uncertain terms that they hoped there would be no opposition to it. On the other hand they expressed considerable disappointment over the fact that the bill does not meet the requests of the Legion.
I presume the government have adopted the attitude that they must under no circumstances grant the full request of any such organization as the Legion. Apparently the government adopted much the same attitude that employers adopt when they go into a collective bargaining deal with the employees. They assume that the employees are asking for more than they expect to get. I am sure hon. members will agree that the requests of the Canadian Legion are very fair. I do not think the Legion asked for more than they expected to get, nor did they ask for more than they felt the veterans were entitled to.
The speeches we have heard in this debate in support of the Legion's request should indicate to the government that the granting of that request will not bring them any unpopularity. The Canadian people will be quite willing to bear the extra expenses that the difference between what is granted and what the veterans asked for will entail.
I am sure every veteran in this country will be a bit disappointed at the maximum amount that can be earned, including war veterans allowance. I just could not follow the minister's argument when he attempted to point out that the ceilings of $1,200 and $2,000 would give those in receipt of veterans allowances some advantage over the veterans receiving 80 per cent and 100 per cent disability pensions. I must confess that I just could not follow his argument there. I just do not see why the veteran who is receiving a small grant by way of veterans allowance should be limited to the maximum which the government pays for disability pensions.
War Veterans Allowance Act
All that a single veteran is permitted to earn over and above his maximum allowance is $10 a month, while the married veteran is allowed to earn $12 per month over and above the $103 maximum allowance. I just cannot see why the line should be drawn there. There is just no inducement for a veteran to go to work for $10 or $12 per month.
We heard the old argument in connection with the ceiling on blind pensions as well as veterans allowances, that the low ceiling gives no encouragement whatever to the veteran in receipt of an allowance to earn anything, granted of course that the new regulation regarding casual earnings will enable a veteran to possibly earn more than that $10 or $12 per month. I want to say here that a number of veterans have expressed to me their appreciation of the liberal interpretation which the Department of Veterans Affairs has placed upon that casual earnings regula-lation. But even allowing for that I support those who ask that the ceiling be raised to that requested by the veterans.
Every time the question of veterans allowance has come up I have opposed the practice of reducing the allowance to the veteran by the amount of old age security which may be received. As has been pointed out again and again, these are about the only group of citizens in the country in connection with whom such an exception is made. There are many in this country in receipt of pensions paid by the government who still retain those pensions or superannuation payments when they reach 70 years of age and obtain the full amount of old age security. I suggest that if the government and the department are not prepared to raise the ceiling as requested by the veterans, they should reconsider the whole question of reducing the veterans allowance when the veteran reaches 70 years of age because he then receives old age security.
I am quite sure that if we are to build up a new army, the kind of army the Department of National Defence is attempting to build up in order to secure this country against possible future war, we must give more consideration to those who fought in the first and second world wars. The sons of those who fought in the second world war will be coming into our new army, as well as the grandsons of those who fought in the first world war. There will be little inducement or encouragement for them to come into the new army when they find their fathers and grandfathers being treated as they are today when they reach the age of 70 years, having the pittance they receive as veterans allowance reduced because they are receiving old age security.

War Veterans Allowance Act
I hope that when the bill comes before the committee the government will call off its whip as far as members of that committee are concerned, so they will have every freedom to make the recommendations they feel are right, and that the government will be guided by the recommendations of the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the unfortunate feature about this bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act is that while it is a help it leaves the very serious war veterans problem only half solved. Hon. members will have noticed that that was the reaction when the resolution preceding the bill was introduced. The minister announced the figures of the increases in the war veterans allowances, and also announced government policy with regard to the ceilings on permissive income. Most of us reacted against the proposals at once on the ground that they were insufficient. It was fairly obvious from the attitude of government supporters that same evening that they too were disappointed in the plans proposed by the minister.
I think there can be no doubt that this debate has shown very clearly where the mistake has been made. I do not intend to go into great detail, because many hon. members have spoken and they have covered the ground very well, but I do want to point out that the increase for the married veteran is insufficient. In the veterans charter which contained the revisions of the different statutes for the benefit of the veteran and which was passed in 1946, we find that the married veteran received twice as much as the single veteran in the way of veterans allowance, and that same proportion is asked for now in the Canadian Legion brief. Hon. members will recall that the Canadian Legion suggested $60 per month for the single veteran and $120 a month for the married veteran. This bill provides $60 a month for the single veteran, but only $1,296 per year for the married veteran. If the married veteran was to be given twice what the single veteran receives he would be allowed $1,440.
A further difficulty in connection with the bill is the amount the veteran is allowed to receive over and above his allowance. I find a great deal of confusion in the terms used to describe this surplus. Sometimes it is called permissive income, and then at another time we find "permissive income" used to describe the allowance plus the amount a man may earn over and above the allowance. I think a suitable phrase to use in describing that amount would be clear income over the war veterans allowance. I believe that would describe more accurately what is meant.

The amount of clear income allowed by the bill is much too low for both the single and married veterans. In the veterans charter this clear income was $125 a year for the single veteran and twice as much, or $250, for the married veteran. Those same figures were continued in the amendment of 1948.
For some reason or other when the War Veterans Allowance Act was revised in 1952 the amount of clear income was reduced to $120 a year both for the single veteran and for the married veteran. That meant they could receive only $10 a month. If I remember correctly those of us in opposition and probably some of the supporters of the government strongly protested at the time because this clear income was being reduced from the figure at which it had been previously.
It will be noticed that before the amendment of 1952 the married veteran had a clear income of a little over $20 a month. In this bill the clear income is to be continued at $120 a year or $10 a month for the single veteran, and $144 a year for the married veteran which amounts to $12 a month. In this latter figure there is an increase of $2.
The Legion is asking for $480 clear income a year for the single veteran and $560 clear income for the married veteran. An amount of $480 a year would of course mean $40 a month, and it would bring the total possible income of a single veteran up to $1,200 a year and the amount of $560 would result in $2,000 a year in the case of a married veteran. As the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) knows, this is the amount in respect of which there is an income tax exemption.
This low standard, this low amount of clear income which has been set by the bill will never be acceptable. The Minister of Veterans Affairs might just as well face that fact now. This low amount of clear income is not going to be acceptable either in this house or outside of it. The veterans of Canada are not going to be satisfied with that amount. Why should they be? If the situation is not properly met at this time it will be fought out session after session until it is properly settled.
Why should the veterans be expected to accept this figure? Let us take for an example the civilian allowance under old age assistance. Under the Old Age Assistance Act the amount of clear income allowed over and above the old age assistance is $240 a year or $20 a month for both single and married people. In this amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act these amounts are only $10 and $12 respectively. In regard to the blind allowance there is a clear income

allowed of $360 a year or $30 a month for both a single and a married person. If both the man and his wife are blind a clear income of $40 a month is allowed. The disability allowance passed by this house just last year allowed a clear income over and above the disability allowance of $240 a year or $20 a month in the case of both a single and a married person. There we have one good reason why the clear income allowed by this amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act will never be accepted in this country.
Again, it will not be accepted because there are at least two large groups in Canada who are severely penalized by the low amount which has been set. The first group is composed of small pensioners who are unable to earn any money. With this low amount of clear income a pensioner can only benefit by reason of his pension to the extent of $10 a month, if he is a single veteran, and to the extent of $12 a month if he is a married veteran, because he is only allowed to receive that much money over and above the amount of his allowance.
The second large group who are penalized are the veterans and the widows of veterans who reach 70 years of age and have no earning power. As a matter of interest I would like to point out that about one-quarter of the recipients of war veterans allowances in Canada today are widows of veterans, and their situation is extremely serious.
I propose to go on and deal with those veterans and widows of veterans who have attained 70 years of age, but I cannot do so in the time that remains. I would ask you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Then I was going on to give another reason why these ceilings would not be satisfactory, in that two large groups of veterans and veterans' widows are heavily 50433-114J
War Veterans Allowance Act penalized by the low amount of clear income. I had dealt with the small pensioner, and had just started to deal with the veteran or the widow of a veteran who reaches the age of 70 and becomes entitled to old age security payments.
I think it is well understood, Mr. Speaker, that when a veteran on war veterans allowance reaches the age of 70 he can benefit by old age security only to the amount of the difference between his allowance and the ceiling of permissive income. That gap has only represented $10 a month in the case of both the single and the married man up to the time of this bill. Now the gap is to be the same $10 for the single man but $12 for the married man.
The result of that provision in effect will be this. The veteran 70 years of age, instead of getting $40 additional in his pocket, or the widow instead of getting $40 additional in her purse, can get only $10. If the veteran is married of course he can get $12, but otherwise there can be only $10 additional come into that man's pocket.
This afternoon the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) said that permissive income does not mean much. He put little value on permissive income. But in the case of the person reaching 70 years of age, permissive income is the whole thing. If this amount of clear income were to be made $40, which would be the same as the old age security payment, then on reaching that age this front-line veteran would continue to get his allowance and, in addition, he would get the $40 old age security. Clearly, I submit, these men and these widows should receive the additional $40 when they reach 70 years of age. That would give them a total income of only $100 a month.
It will be only a few years, perhaps 10 or 12, until practically every veteran who served in the first world war will be 70 years of age. I believe the average age now is about 64 or 65. Certainly in another 15 years every single veteran who served in the first world war and who has entitlement to the war veterans allowance will be over 70 years of age. Hence this question of whether he is to get $40 additional upon reaching the age of 70 is of vital importance, and it will become of more importance each year. In asking for a total permissible income of $1,200 for the single veteran, the Legion had that point in mind, namely that when he reached 70 years of age he would get his war veterans allowance of $60 and the old age security payment of $40.
The special committee on veterans affairs might well consider whether it would not

War Veterans Allowance Act now be wise to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act to take old age security payments right out, to exempt them from consideration as income. Under section 6 of the act we have mentioned different types of incomes that are exempt or, in other words, that are not taken into consideration at all in arriving at income for purposes of the act. For example, they ignore any money received by a widow as mothers' allowance from one of the provinces; and family allowance payments are not considered in deciding the income for purposes of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Other exemptions also are now written into the act. If the government will not raise this ceiling so there is a clear income of $40 a month, an alternative way of dealing with the situation might be to write into this section 6 the provision that old age security payments shall not count as income. That would take care of all the veterans when they reach the age of 70.
Another reason this low amount of clear income will never be satisfactory can be deduced from the findings of two previous committees on veterans affairs. For example, in 1952 the committee of that year recommended as follows:
Your committee further recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans allowance, keeping in mind the recommendations of veterans organizations in that respect and particularly with regard to permissive income.
The committee of that year, in mentioning permissive income specifically, had in mind this difference between the amount of the allowance and the amount a veteran could receive in his pocket. A similar recommendation was contained in the report of the committee last year. They made the recommendation that the government should give further consideration to the briefs of the veterans organizations, and particularly to the raising of the amounts of the allowances and also the raising of the levels of permissive income. That committee dealt with two different aspects of the subject, namely raising the allowances and raising the amount of clear income that a veteran could receive. Now this bill deals with the one and not with the other. There is an absolute failure to deal with the question of clear income.
When he spoke, the minister talked of the war veterans allowance assistance fund. I point out to him and to the house that that fund operates only as between the allowance and the ceiling. In other words it cannot bring the money in pocket over and above the ceiling. Hence under this bill in the case of the single veteran the most help he can get is the difference between $60 and the $70 which is fixed as a ceiling. Furthermore


the war veterans allowance assistance fund would be of practically no help to the veteran or the widow over 70 years of age, or to most of the small pensioners because what they get from old age security or from a small pension brings them up to the ceiling. Therefore the assistance fund is of no use to these two very large groups.
It should also not be forgotten that there is a second means test involved in the war veterans allowance assistance fund. To get such assistance the veteran has to be put on the griddle a second time. Inquiries have to be made all about his position and his assets, and it is only in a case where the veteran is suffering great hardship that he is able to get any assistance from the fund. The very fact that an assistance fund is required shows the absolute inadequacy of the allowance itself. If the Legion's recommendation of $120 a month for the married veteran were to be implemented there would be no requirement for an assistance fund at all, and a great deal of administrative difficulty would be avoided.
These are some of the reasons why the bill will not be accepted as a solution of the war veterans allowance problem. I think the minister and his parliamentary assistant have been made to realize that fact very clearly by the course the debate has taken. They should realize now that the fight for justice for these front-line fighting men must go on. This fight is only starting. It will be continued until we get a proper gap between the amount of the allowance and the amount the veteran can receive into his pocket by way of income.

Throughout this whole debate, Mr. Speaker, I have been somewhat disillusioned. For years I had been given to understand that the 31st won the war; later, it was the 75th, and now I find a lot of other fellows who seem to have had something to do with it. I distinctly recall that some months ago the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) said it was not the purpose of the opposition to compliment the government. I, therefore, want to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra for taking that attitude, and letting them know what is our purpose in life.
While I have spoken to some extent on this subject already, I have a few things to say now that I believe merit some consideration. First, I am appreciative of what the minister has done in this particular effort. For his benefit I may say that despite what our good friends have said about receiving telegrams, I have not received a telegram from my constituency so far. However, that does not mean that everybody is in agreement on this bill. I feel the minister is as much aware of that as I am. I expect I shall probably hear from my community, but if I do not I shall act accordingly.
As I understand it, the main purpose in creating the war veterans allowance was to look after the burnt-out veterans. I believe


that is a very important consideration, because we should not forsake them completely. I note that the proposed increase amounts to $120 per year in the case of a single man and $144 per year in the case of a married man. I should like to draw to the minister's attention the fact that this means we consider the increase in the cost of living for a single man amounts to $120, while the increased cost in the case of a married couple would be $72 per individual. I do not believe the minister can justify setting the per unit costs for a family of two people at 10 per cent less than for a single individual. The cost does not work in that ratio.
As I pointed out on an earlier occasion, I feel that the difference of $2 between what is offered to the single man and what is offered to the married war veteran is a niggardly sum. How can we expect them to live on less than the amount received by old age pensioners in my province or the province of Alberta? I should like the minister to seriously reconsider that phase of the matter. When the committee is set up the members should try and reconcile in their own minds the fact that in Alberta and British Columbia old age pensioners receive $110 per month for a family of two, while under this scheme a couple will only receive $108. It is not a matter of the $2, it is the principle that is involved in the whole thing.
It is going to be most difficult for any man to explain to the people of this country why we should differentiate. While the minister has said he has given an increase of 20 per cent in the original veterans allowance right across the board, in this case I would say the veterans' brief should have been considered on its merits. Some adjustment is going to have to be made during the committee stage in so far as a married couple is concerned.
The other factor is the failure to increase permissible income. In my community, and I imagine it is true across Canada, I find that society requires the burnt-out veteran who is capable of doing a few hours' work per week. We have community halls and other places that need janitors, and there are other vocations open to him. We need these people. We cannot afford to pay a man full time to look after some of these things, and it is helpful to be able to obtain someone for $50 per month. This would mean $600 per year and the veteran is permitted an income of $840, which would mean he would automatically lose $480 of the $600 he had earned. I contend that is quite unreasonable. I see no excuse at all for doing so, and I do not see why an individual should not be permitted an income of $1,200 per year if single or $2,000

per year if married. I do not think that is an unreasonable request on the part of the veterans at all.
The minister has said that it would mean $5 million a year, and our good friend the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), who so often interjects his ideas into these debates, has called that peanuts. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) says that in this instance that is peanut shells. Let us give these veterans that consideration.
In the matter of perquisites, too, we are most unrealistic. If a man happens to have an extra quart of milk from his cow it does not make any sense that he should be told to throw it out because if he sells it to his neighbour that amount will be deducted from his allowance. To put it bluntly, that is asinine. I believe the human element should be taken into consideration. I realize it is quite impractical to try to put all these things in a bill, but there should be a greater degree of licence given to those who administer the act to enable them to take care of this human element.
I heartily agree with the minister's idea of increasing war veterans allowances. The principle of the thing is important, and I compliment him for introducing it, but I am not happy with some of the proposals.

Consider who they are. Their age has been described, and the sufferings they endured in the first war. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is competent to do it as perhaps nobody else is, because he is one of the few men who was a front-line soldier in both wars. When he dared to say, as I would not have dared to say, that the men of the second war did not go through the gruelling experiences of the men in the trenches in the first war, then I accepted that at its face value. When I found that those men, in his words-and I take his word for it-are to be discriminated against, then it seems to me that is something intolerable, something we in this house should not put up with.
I want to add this. I would think it is quite arguable that it is the best men who are suffering most, and I would like to underline that for just a moment. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre pointed out to me today what I suppose I should have recalled, that when the time came to leave England men wanted one thing, to get home; they did not want to stay on, to establish pension conditions. They wanted to get home, and so many of them lost the opportunity.
I might be forgiven for perhaps mentioning one instance that comes to my mind very vividly. We had in the 9th battery that I was in originally a very fine sergeant. I remember quite well that he suffered an injury, but the last thing in the world he wanted was to make any claim on the public purse. He was still young. He thought he would be able to look after himself; but 20 years later he came into my office one day and he said this to me: "Do you remember that night we came into Plug Street? We were on the gun wheel. You were pulling on one side of the wheel; I was hoisting on the other. Do you remember that I said to you: 'I felt something give in my back'?" I said to him, "My dear fellow, that was 20 years ago. If you had asked me the next day or the next week, I could have remembered, but I cannot remember now. Nobody would believe me if I said I could remember now".
The only reason I am using that instance is to point out that here is a man who presumably lost his pension rights because he did not want to tap the public purse. He wanted to look after himself. I am sorry to say that I do not know his plight today. He may very likely be one of those who is going to be discriminated against, and it is that I want to protest against. That is all I want to say. I hope the committee will not allow that.

War Veterans Allowance Act
It is often my duty in this house to protest against expenditures, and I hope I shall have many chances to do it in future; but there are times when we should not economize. There are times when we should not hesitate to do what is right whatever the cost; and if I am stating the case correctly then I cannot understand how men, veterans like myself on the opposite side of the house, hesitate to say what I am trying to say now. If it is true that these men are being discriminated against, then all I can say is that it is a disgrace to every one of us which we should not tolerate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to close this debate on the motion for second reading of the bill I should like to express to hon. members, as I have done on previous occasions in similar debates, my appreciation for their participation in this debate.
As I have said before, I believe that discussions of the various problems having to do with the responsibilities of my department serve a very useful purpose. From those discussions and that exchange of ideas over a great many years has emerged the veterans charter as we have it today. And certainly, sir, if any useful purpose is to be served by a debate or discussion on the points at issue, then it has been accomplished because we have had two days of debate on the second reading of the bill and a day on the resolution which preceded the introduction of the bill.
I do not want to go over every one of the points which have been raised by hon. members. As I said before, and as the house knows, the bill is to be referred to the special committee on veterans affairs, and much of the information which hon. members wish to seek can be obtained there and discussed more usefully in the committee. However, there are certain points which I should like to make tonight in closing this debate.
I think we will all agree that in the debate the general criticism has been on the proposed income ceilings for recipients of war veterans allowance. Some discussion has taken place on the rates themselves, but generally speaking the criticism has been on the ceilings. Some hon. members have gone to great pains to explain to the house that the ceiling increases which are in the bill before the house at the present time are not increases at all, that no increase of the income ceiling has been granted.

I do not want to go into a detailed analysis of that particular point, but according to my arithmetic-and I cannot help thinking according to everybody else's arithmetic-an increase from $720 to $840 is an increase of $120, and an increase in the ceiling from $1,200 to $1,440 is an increase of $240. What it does mean is that the single recipient of war veterans allowance, after this bill has been put into force, will be permitted to have $840 whereas he had only $720 before; and that a married recipient will be able to have $1,440 whereas he could have only $1,200 before. It seems to me, in the final analysis, that is what really matters to the veteran.
As I say, I do not wish to labour this point; but it does appear to me that the discussion of this particular point has revealed-well, I would not like to say ignorance, but certainly a complete disregard of the legislation and of the regulations as they exist now.
I do not know that I blame hon. members too much. Reading the editorial which appeared in the last issue of The Legionary, from which some hon. members have quoted profusely, I was surprised to find in it an argument which would seem to justify what has been expressed by my hon. friends. I certainly do not want to take issue with the editor of The Legionary, particularly with regard to this editorial which in part commends the minister and the government. I must admit that is the sort of treatment which I am not too accustomed to receiving from this publication, and I certainly would not want to antagonize the editor. I should like to read the paragraph which some hon. members have quoted. After having discussed the rates and how helpful the increase will be to the recipients, the editor goes on to say:
The increase from $1,200 to only $1,440 in the total permissible income for married recipients and from $720 to only $840 for single men should also be reconsidered. Many of these ageing veterans, while incapable of taking steady jobs, can do part-time work and thus augment their incomes. It seems unreasonable to deny them the right to help themselves, if able to do so, to achieve something in their declining years which at least approaches a decent standing of living;-
That is exactly the point I was trying to make. In expressing such views today I know that hon. members did so most sincerely. Some hon. members said that everything should be done to encourage these recipients of war veterans allowances to work when they are capable of doing so, in order to increase their income by taking part-time work. In other words they should try to help themselves.

This has been in the act since the amendments of 1952. By the introduction of section 4, which now exists, we permit recipients of war veterans allowances to do exactly what is asked in this article. By the amendment last year of the definition of casual earnings we permitted greater scope to the activities in which recipients of war veterans allowances could participate in order to increase their income by part-time work. With section 4 as it exists today and with the definition of casual earnings as it exists today, almost everything except full-time regular employment is accepted and the veteran can derive income from that type of work.

I have been listening for two days to hon. members, and I wish they would permit me to make my point. I shall be glad to answer questions afterwards.
Last year, I think at the demand of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, I placed on Hansard the definition of casual earnings. If hon. members will refer to Hansard of last year they will see that almost any type of part-time work can be taken by these recipients of war veterans allowances, and that earnings therefrom will not be considered as income for the purposes of this act. Or they can take full-time employment of a temporary nature with the same result. Under the amendments brought forward we are still permitting the recipient of war veterans allowance to increase his income to whatever amount he can by means of outside work under section 4 or through casual earnings.
That deals with the recipient who can supplement his income by casual earnings, who can take part-time work or who can obtain temporary full-time employment. How about the man who cannot do that, the man who has absolutely nothing but his war veterans allowance; the man who has no outside income, who is completely unable to work even at part-time work or to enjoy casual earnings? Under the proposed rates which have been mentioned here by hon. members, and the changes suggested in the brief of the Canadian Legion, a married man would receive $120 a month or $1,440 a year, and the permissive income would be raised to $2,000. But I am now referring to the man who has no outside income, who cannot go out and earn anything on the side. Such a man would be receiving $1,440 and nothing else.
Under the amendments provided by this bill he will receive $108 a month or $1,296 a year. But as I explained before, we are continuing the assistance fund and through the medium of that fund, which is to be operated
War Veterans Allowance Act under a new formula, this same man could have his allowance increased from $108 to $120 a month, or $1,440 a year, which is exactly the amount mentioned in the brief submitted by the Legion.
How about the single man? According to the requests which have been placed before us the single man would receive $60 a month. This has been granted. His ceiling by way of permissible income was to be $1,200. I am still dealing with the man who has no outside income, who cannot take any outside work. Under the proposals of the Canadian Legion this single recipient would get $60 a month and not a cent more. Under our plan he gets $60 a month and he would be entitled to another $10 per month from the assistance fund, which is $10 more than the Legion asked for.
Those are the exact figures to be found in the bill. I do not know what more I can say. As I said, the new definition of casual earnings permits a recipient to go out and earn almost any amount as long as it is not at regular, full-time employment.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) and the hon. member for Okan-agan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) referred to the recipient of war veterans allowance who is living on a bit of land and who had to account for his perquisites, as it used to be defined in the act. That situation does not exist any longer. At the same time we changed the definition of casual earnings last year we changed the definition of farm income. Perquisites are not taken into consideration, and the definition of farm income which was adopted was the one suggested to us by various veterans organizations.
There again, Mr. Speaker, I think it is a very generous provision. Briefly, this is what is to be assessed as income. Twenty-five per cent of the first $1,000 of the gross farm income, 40 per cent of the next $1,000 of gross farm income and 50 per cent of the balance of the gross farm income. I think that is a generous formula. If the veteran prefers, and it is up to him to make the choice, he can have his net income determined and use that for the purpose of war veterans allowance. I believe the recipients of war veterans allowance who are living in rural districts are in a better position, generally speaking, than those who are living in urban centres. I think those veterans who are living in rural districts and farming in a small way are being treated very well indeed under the new definition.
I was extremely pleased, Mr. Speaker, to hear some hon. members say during the course of this debate that they realize we are all responsible to the taxpayer for the
1798	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act expenditure of his money. A number of hon. members said this, and I must say that I cannot recall any previous debate concerning veterans affairs in which I have participated when such a statement was made. It is a correct statement to make, because one cannot escape the fact, as mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that, desirable as these changes might be, the money has to be found to pay for them and the taxpayer is the one who eventually pays.
I would be very pleased indeed if the situation were as suggested by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, that the Liberal party has a private fund from which it could provide for these increases. Unfortunately such a fund does not exist. I can assure my hon. friend that if there were such a fund I would be the most generous member of this party.
Suggestions have been made this afternoon as to how such funds could be raised. The hon. member for Oxford suggested there might be a curtailment of the construction of public buildings, which could provide the necessary funds. I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) can well defend his policy concerning public buildings. I cannot resist saying, however, that I recall that during the debate on the speech from the throne, the consideration of the estimates of public works or the budget debate the hon. members of the opposition were not the least hesitant in asking for the erection of public buildings in their respective constituencies.

Mr. Speaker, I am not rising to oppose this motion. As a matter of fact I am strongly in favour of it as, I am sure, are all members of the house. The motion has now been on the order paper for some time, and in the last few days we have had a lengthy debate on war veterans allowances. I may say that it has been an extremely interesting debate. The bill has now been given second reading, and it will go before this committee for consideration. I know all hon. members who expect to be on that committee are extremely anxious to get to work on the bill.
This is the usual resolution that is moved to set up a veterans affairs committee. In addition to the bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act I note that the committee will be asked to consider a bill to amend the Veterans Benefit Act, 1954, and such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred to it from time to time. I thought possibly the minister might give us some indication of what other legislation will be coming before the committee. I also note that the committee is to consist of 31 members, which is the same number we had on the committee last year. I have no objection to the number, though I may say that in this house there are so many veterans of two wars that it is difficult to recommend members for the committee inasmuch as practically every war veteran in the House of Commons is anxious to sit on a veterans affairs committee. In 1946, when we had the veterans charter before a veterans affairs committee, the committee consisted of some 60 members, I believe. Practically all the veterans in the house were on that committee.
In this debate we have had during the last few days, after listening to some of the speeches made by hon. members in this house some of us might begin to wonder just whether there would be much benefit in setting up a committee at all. However, I am like the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra: I have sat on a good many veterans affairs committees. I have seen a good many bills come before veterans affairs committees. Some I have seen passed without any change, but to many I have seen amendments and changes made. After all, Mr. Speaker, I think that is the purpose of a committee. There would be absolutely no object at all in setting up a special committee on veterans affairs or a special committee to consider any other bill of any department if that committee were simply to act as a rubber stamp, if our minds were made up beforehand on
1800	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Veterans Affairs all the principles of the bill, and if we followed the suggestions that were laid down in the bill prior to it coming before the committee.
In a special committee we have an opportunity which we do not have here in the house. For instance, we have the opportunity of hearing veterans organizations from across Canada. They know the situation of the ex-soldier far better than many of us know it and can tell us that. They know the requirements and the needs. Their representations help us to form our opinions. In addition, we shall also have opinions from the departmental officials. It is necessary to get all the facts in a matter of this kind before making our decisions. We can also find out just what are the costs of any changes. As I said a moment ago, I feel that it is a splendid thing that a bill of this kind goes before a special committee. It is only proper that all members on that committee should have an open mind with regard to what is to be discussed before it.
I might take this opportunity to suggest, as I have suggested on many other occasions, that we should have a permanent committee on veterans affairs. No doubt that sounds like an old chestnut, because it is something that has been advocated time and time again here in the house. The fact that we had a veterans affairs committee last year, that we are to have another veterans affairs committee this year, and that in the last 20 years we have had many veterans affairs committees would indicate to me, as I think it should to the government, that it is necessary indeed to set up a permanent committee on veterans affairs.
For instance, this year the estimates of the veterans affairs department are going before a special committee on estimates. If we had a permanent committee on veterans affairs that committee, along with the other business which might be put before it, could very well discuss and review the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
When I say that, I realize that the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs possibly need less scrutiny than do the estimates of some of the other departments of government, because they are the estimates in which we are all greatly interested. They deal with pensions. No one is desirous of lowering the pensions of our pensioners in Canada. They deal with the war veterans allowance. After listening to this debate for the last two or three days, I am sure no one would suggest that we are anxious to reduce the estimates for war veterans allowances. Then there is hospitalization. No one wishes to reduce the


estimates for hospitalization. These are estimates which perhaps do not require the same degree of scrutiny as the estimates of other departments.
It is not my intention to prolong this debate. We are very anxious to see the committee established. I am sure those of us who expect to be members of the committee are looking forward to it, and I am sure that when the bills come before the committee we will not be expected to act as rubber stamps, no matter which side of the house we are on, but will give every section of the bills the most sincere consideration.

I should like to support the suggestions made by the members who have just spoken with regard to this resolution, Mr. Speaker. If the veterans affairs estimates are to be considered by the estimates committee, and they have already been referred to that committee, then we shall probably have the situation that the estimates committee is dealing with the estimates of veterans affairs while the special committee on veterans affairs is dealing only with the legislation; that is all the power given to the special committee under this resolution. It would seem to be a businesslike procedure, now that we are to have a special committee on veterans affairs, to allow that committee to deal with the estimates.
What use would it be to have another committee, which has an entirely new approach to these questions, dealing with the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs? If the special committee were allowed to discuss them, then such questions as the Veterans Land Act or any other questions that come up under the estimates could be discussed. These problems are of a type quite different from the ordinary problems which face the house.
The estimates committee, in dealing with northern affairs or finance department estimates, or even citizenship and immigration estimates, has a different sort of problems to handle. Here in veterans affairs we have a very specialized field. It is a field which will continue for many, many years. Surely this is the time at least to try out the plan of having veterans affairs estimates considered by this special committee. As the minister knows we have followed a similar practice with external affairs estimates for about ten years now.
