speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved:
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting; that the committee shall consist of the following members:	Messrs. Balcer, Beaudry,
Boisvert, Bryson, Carter, Cauchon, Decore, Diefen-baker, Dinsdale, Fleming, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gauthier (Nickel Belt), Goode, Hansell, Henry, Holowach, Kirk (Shelburne - Yarmouth - Clare), Knight, McCann, Monteith, Reinke, Richard (Ottawa East), Richardson, Robichaud, Studer, Weaver; that standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: I am glad to have this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of moving the appointment of the committee on broadcasting. We have thought it is a good thing to have such a committee of the house every year or so, as was convenient. I believe it has always been widely agreed that there are special reasons for the appointment of a committee on broadcasting. Because of the nature of broadcasting the C.B.C. has been placed by statute in a position in which it is not responsible to a minister of the crown in carrying out its activities. It is answerable to parliament itself. Quite differently from my own department, for instance, I am not responsible for the general activities of the C.B.C. There are many of them about which I could not readily inform the house. Altogether, it does seem particularly appropriate that the house should appoint a committee to examine the activities and policies of the corporation, and consider general broadcasting matters.
The government, of course, has to develop general policies regarding broadcasting and, from time to time, must lay before parliament proposals regarding broadcasting and the methods of providing revenues. The licensing of stations, for instance, comes directly under the government, although the board of governors of the C.B.C. makes recommendations regarding applications.
7. 1955	1803
Special Committee on Broadcasting
I imagine the committee will wish to devote a great deal of attention to television broadcasting. I should like to emphasize the immense importance of television to our families and to the national life of Canada. We are rapidly approaching the point when the majority of Canadian homes will have television sets. We all know that most families having sets spend a good deal of time each week watching them. I know there are people who do not like television, or prefer to try to ignore it as of no importance, but no thinking person can ignore something which is playing an increasingly important part in the lives and thoughts of a growing number of Canadians.
The over-all pattern of material appearing on television screens throughout the country during the next few years will have a great effect on the mental attitudes of most Canadians a generation from now. The degree to which television draws on and stimulates Canadian ideas and abilities and exchange of information will be no small factor in our nationhood in the years ahead. I believe we in parliament have to realize that ultimately we have the over-all responsibility for what television brings into the Canadian home, and what its relationship is to our general national life. It is not enough to say, let there be television, and to license any first-comers to broadcast. We have to face the hard facts that apply.
Production of television programs, for instance, is expensive and complicated. In Canada it is in general far cheaper to import program material than to produce it in this country. We have only a fraction of the people of, say, the United States to support production costs. Yet if television is to contribute anything much to our national life it surely must include a substantial amount of programming of different kinds done by Canadians for Canadians.
Furthermore, we are a country of two languages and from the beginning we have had to duplicate program production. While our population is relatively small, our geographic size is very great. Therefore the cost of transmitting and distributing programs to Canadians in different parts of the country is extremely high. I am sure we all agree that television should help to join together Canadians who live in different regions, and that it should assist in that way to a better common understanding.
The last committee on broadcasting strongly recommended that television be developed in such a way as to make possible a substantial production of Canadian programs, and the nation-wide distribution of program service. It urged that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and privately owned
1804	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting stations join together in an over-all system working in partnership toward those aims. The policy of the government has been in line with the recommendations of the committee. In its licensing of private stations and its authorizing of C.B.C. facilities the government has sought the ends which the committee felt were important.
Our aim has been to see the development of a nation-wide system, including both privately and publicly owned elements, as needed, capable of assuring the production of at least a fair degree of Canadian programming and extending coverage to as many different parts of the country as possible. We have consistently tried to take a wide national view, thinking in so far as practical of all different parts of the country and endeavouring to assure service as equal as could be achieved in different main areas.
Under this policy the development of television in Canada has been very rapid during the last two years. There are already 25 television stations in operation. Of these 7 are owned by the C.B.C. and 18 by private interests. At the present time five more stations are under construction, one by the C.B.C. and four by private licensees. All these stations, both publicly and privately owned, carry national program service and extend the coverage of the national system. Each station that goes on the air makes television available to more Canadians who did not have it previously. Altogether over 70 per cent of the whole population of Canada is now within coverage of the system.
I think it is indicative of both public interest in television and the success of the system in providing acceptable service that over a million and a quarter television sets have been sold in Canada, nearly all of them since Canadian television started just over two and a half years ago. It is estimated that at the present time over 30 per cent of Canadian households actually have television receivers, and the number is continuing to grow rapidly. Altogether the estimate is that Canadians have spent about half a billion dollars on television receiving equipment. That shows in terms of dollars how interested Canadians are in television. It also demonstrates that television has provided a very important stimulus to business activity in the country during the past two years.
Hon. members may not realize that in the short space of two years Canada in a number of ways has become the second television country in the world. It is, for instance, second in the number of stations. It is second in terms of the area over which television service is available. It is probably close to being second, with the United Kingdom, in


the proportion of the population that have television sets, and it is a good third in the total number of sets in homes. It is probably particularly surprising to know that it is second among the nations at present in the amount of program production carried on. This is, of course, related to the fact that from the beginning we have had full program service and program production in two different languages.
These facts emphasize the intensity of the development during the past two and a half years, but still more they indicate the size of the job which Canadian conditions set in television. In spite of the high number of stations and the comparatively large amount of total production we already have, there is still a long way to go in extending coverage in many areas and in development of our own programming.
I think hon. members are aware that all private stations carry a considerable amount of national program service provided by the C.B.C. either through direct network connection or by means of television recordings. In this way the C.B.C., through these private stations, gets service to viewers in their areas. The cost is considerable to the C.B.C. for service through each such station, but it is still of course much cheaper than if the C.B.C. itself established stations in all these areas. On the other hand, through this system we have in Canada private stations obtain considerable programming through the C.B.C. at no cost, and at the same time get some revenue in respect of the commercial network programs they carry.
To me this is a very sensible form of co-operation in facing the great problems posed in television by the nature of our country. I think we can say actually there is in effect and working well the kind of partnership in this field envisaged by the last parliamentary committee. I should like here to say a word of tribute to the private stations who with the C.B.C. have pioneered in the building up of nation-wide television in Canada.
I believe this co-operation between public and private enterprise in this field makes very good sense in Canada. Indeed, I think it is the only sensible way of meeting the challenge that Canadian conditions set in television. The public component of the system, the C.B.C., is essential to assure the production of any real amount of Canadian programming, which is just not practical on a straight commercial basis. The C.B.C., too, has the job of assuring the nation-wide distribution of national program service, including imported material as well as that produced in Canada.

This linking of the country by a great east-west distribution system again has to be a public responsibility, in the sense that pure commercial considerations would not support it. The C.B.C. has the minimum number of stations and production centres to assure a fair degree of Canadian program production, some in other regions of the country as well as in Montreal and Toronto. Private stations have had opportunities to go ahead in many other areas of the country, and the figures show that they have done so willingly. In this way there has been plenty of room for private enterprise in television, and to some extent there has been assistance for it. The owners of private stations have wide opportunities for their own initiative as well as for their responsibilities as affiliates of the national system, a responsibility which I understand they are in general willingly carrying out.
The system we have provides for an integration of resources toward meeting our national aims. The support comes from different sources; from moneys paid by the television-viewing public directly; from commercial activities of the C.B.C. and the whole system acting as a network; from the investment and initiative and activities of the private station owners. All these are channelled together to support our developing television system, and all are essential.
I believe our television system is one of the biggest developments in the history of Canada. Such things as east-west pipe lines can be very important to our economy, but in television we are dealing with something which is not only a great economic stimulus; still far more important, it produces and carries across the country things for people's minds. I feel it is vital for Canada that through the years we develop a system that effectively joins together the different parts of Canada from one coast to the other, and that in good part consists of Canadian ideas and information and talent.
I think in connection with television we in this house should take a wide national view. I know it is very easy for anyone to sit before a television set and have strong personal views about what they see. It is not so easy to think about television service, or the lack of it, in quite another part of the country, or to think about all the economic factors that apply to the production and distribution of television programs.
There may be some hon. members, for instance, who feel it is urgent to licence additional stations in some particular areas of the country where there is already service. I suppose that most television viewers, if asked if they would like to have another
7, 1955	1805
Special Committee on Broadcasting station to choose from, would naturally tend to say yes. But they would not be thinking of the great integration of resources through both public and private and commercial channels which is necessary in Canada to maintain and develop a nation-wide television system with a minimum amount of Canadian production. I think we should be careful about moving too quickly in some special areas to permit duplicate service which would inevitably tend to weaken the strength and growing power of the national system as a whole, consisting of public and private stations stretching all across the country.
We must remember that our television system is still at a very early stage of development. It is only two and a half years old. During the last year particularly it has grown very quickly and the growth is still continuing at a rapid rate. A great deal has still to be done. I think most people will agree, including the C.B.C. itself, I know, that there is need for considerable improvement and development in the programming. There are still a great many areas of the country and a considerable proportion of the population not within reach of television coverage.
Whether such coverage of the national system is extended through private stations or through relay stations to be owned by the C.B.C., there are still costs to be met. A pressing need is for direct relay network connection among stations across the country. As hon. members are aware, all the stations in operation at present between Windsor, Ontario, and Quebec city are joined in a direct relay network by microwave systems. Programs are supplied to stations in other parts of the country by means of television recordings. The use of recordings has always been envisaged by the C.B.C. only as a substitute until a direct network system could be established. The use of recordings means considerable delay in the viewing of programs in other parts of the country, and also inferior technical quality for viewers in those areas.
The C.B.C. has been working on this matter for some time, and some months ago called for tenders for extensions of the direct network from the two main national communications groups, the railway-telegraph companies working together on one hand, and the telephone companies of the country associated in the trans-Canada telephone system on the other hand. Following study of the tenders the corporation has proposed to accept the tenders of the telephone companies for the extension of the English language network service west from Toronto to Vancouver and east from Montreal as

Special Committee on Broadcasting far as Sydney, Nova Scotia, and to accept the tender of the railway-telegraph companies for extensions of the French network service within the province of Quebec. The tenders accepted were the lowest in each case. This awarding of contracts has been submitted for approval by order in council, as required by the Canadian Broadcasting Act.

speechtext: May I ask the minister if he intends to table the order in council?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It has not been passed.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: When it is.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When it is we will table it. It is referred by the C.B.C. to the government for authority. According to the act all expenditures over a certain amount must come before the government.
The microwave systems are of course built in each case by the communications companies themselves. Under the contracts the C.B.C. would pay annual amounts. The contracts would cover direct service by microwave to all stations now in operation or authorized right from Vancouver to Sydney. Under the contracts the C.B.C. has rights for ten years, and the annual basic amounts involved would be close to $2 million. Against this the corporation will have some offsetting amounts in savings on its present recording service and in additional commercial revenues. It is expected that the complete coast to coast service will be in operation in about three years, with portions to be completed well before that.
I think the establishment of this direct relay system right across the country is a major step forward in our television system and in communication in general among Canadians. It will mean that all across Canada people will be able to see many of the same programs simultaneously and having comparable quality. I think it will help in a great way to bring different regions of Canada closer together.
I have never tried to hide from the house the fact that television is very expensive. For instance, as I am sure hon. members are aware, almost anything in television costs from five to ten times as much as the parallel thing in sound broadcasting. I have always made it plain that in one way or another television broadcasting will cost the Canadian public a good deal of money. Yet while the sums involved in television broadcasting are large, and will grow still larger, they do not seem so great when compared with the quarter of a billion dollars which Canadians spent on television receiving equipment last year alone.


I am sure the committee will wish to examine expenditures of the C.B.C. on television and consider the financial implications involved in television development. We shall have to weigh expenditures and commitments carefully, but we also must consider what I believe to be of great importance, the developing and keeping of television in Canada on a basis that will enable it to contribute as it should to our national life.
The committee will undoubtedly also wish to consider activities and questions related to sound broadcasting. In the last two years there have not been major developments in this field, but even with the development of television sound broadcasting still has an extremely important role.
As mentioned to the last committee, the corporation has proceeded with the establishment of a French language broadcasting station in New Brunswick, at Moncton, and has for the first time set up its own studios in Saskatchewan, at Regina. It has also extended coverage considerably in a number of outlying areas chiefly through low power relay transmitters connected by land lines with national networks.
As well as reviewing sound broadcasting activities of the C.B.C., the committee will probably wish to give consideration to some of the questions arising in the light of television development. It does seem to me that sound broadcasting will continue to have a very important part for as long ahead as we can foresee. It is especially important in more outlying areas and there are still parts of Canada which receive no radio service, or a service which is quite inadequate. An important question is the possibility of the provision of regular, dependable radio service in areas of northern Canada where there is a good deal of development. This could only be undertaken at considerable expense, but I think the committee may wish to study some of the needs and possibilities.
As hon. members are aware, the operation of the international service is on a different basis from the national system of the C.B.C. In effect the C.B.C. acts as an agent for the government in carrying on the shortwave broadcasting service to other nations. The policies and scope of expenditures of the international service are set by the government, and funds for it are provided in annual estimates submitted by the government to parliament.
Hon. members will have noticed that the estimates for this service are considerably reduced for the coming fiscal year. As the house is aware, we have been making strenuous efforts to keep government expenditures down and make savings where possible.

In the light of the need for a general cutting of expenditures a thorough study of the international service was made earlier this year. It was decided that a considerable saving could be made by dropping the regular daily services to a number of western European countries whom we generally regard as friendly to Canada and well disposed to our way of thinking.
It was also decided that with the present state of the world, services to countries behind the iron curtain should not be reduced but should be continued with the same effort, as part of the general endeavour by the countries of the west to get some rays of true information to people under communist domination.
With the dropping of the daily services to western European countries some better broadcasting time will be available for the eastern European language service. The regular Latin-Ameriean service is being continued on a somewhat reduced scale. I think it is regrettable in many ways that we should have to lose our daily contacts with the apparently quite considerable audiences for Canadian broadcasting in the Scandinavian countries, The Netherlands and Italy.
Business of the House It is hoped to retain some connection and some of the good will that has been built up through programs broadcast on week ends and possibly some sent for direct relay by broadcasting systems in the countries themselves.
I think that this year, as in other years, the committee will wish to examine the operations of the international service, as well as the national sound and television operations of the C.B.C. itself.
